The 'Great Attractor' is a gravitational anomaly toward which the Milky Way and millions of nearby galaxies are flowing at ~600 km/s. Located at a distance of about 250 million light-years in the direction of Centaurus, it is now understood to be the Norma Cluster and the broader Shapley Supercluster complex, the largest concentration of galaxies in the nearby universe.

Recurrent novae have the shortest recurrence times of any known nova class. RS Ophiuchi has erupted at least six times since 1898 (1898, 1933, 1958, 1985, 2006, 2021), with the white dwarf accumulating enough hydrogen from its red giant companion to detonate roughly every 15–20 years. It is a candidate for a future Type Ia supernova if the white dwarf mass grows above the Chandrasekhar limit.

The cosmic expansion can be understood through Hubble's law: v = H0 × d, where galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. For very distant objects, recession velocities can exceed the speed of light — not violating special relativity because it is space itself expanding, not objects moving through space. The proper distance to the observable horizon is increasing faster than c.

The Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and South Pole Telescope (SPT) observe the CMB at arcminute resolution, resolving individual galaxy clusters via the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, detecting CMB lensing by large-scale structure, and constraining the sum of neutrino masses and the number of effective relativistic species at percent-level precision.

The Cepheid period-luminosity relation has two significant systematic calibration uncertainties: photometric zero points and metallicity corrections. The SH0ES (Supernova H0 for the Equation of State) program has refined the Cepheid calibration using the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes and consistently finds H0 ~ 73 km/s/Mpc, in tension with the Planck value.

The Jeans instability criterion determines when a gas cloud will collapse under gravity. It depends on the ratio of gravitational potential energy to thermal kinetic energy: collapse occurs when the cloud's mass exceeds the Jeans mass. In the present universe, star-forming molecular clouds need to cool sufficiently for this condition to be met, which is why cold dense molecular clouds are the birthplaces of stars.

Subgiant stars are stars that have begun evolving off the main sequence as their core hydrogen is exhausted; they brighten and cool slightly, lying above the main sequence on the H-R diagram. Subgiant ages can be precisely determined via their position on the H-R diagram, making them invaluable 'stellar clocks' for calibrating the overall age scale of the Milky Way.

The Lunar Laser Ranging experiment, established during the Apollo missions and still operating today, bounces laser pulses off retroreflectors left on the Moon's surface. By measuring the round-trip time with nanosecond precision, scientists monitor the Moon's recession, test the equivalence principle, and constrain changes in the gravitational constant to better than 1 part in 10^13 per year.

Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are eruptions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona, releasing up to 10^24 joules of energy. The fastest CMEs travel at 3,000 km/s and can reach Earth in under 15 hours. When their magnetic field orientation is southward (antiparallel to Earth's field), they efficiently connect to Earth's magnetosphere, causing strong geomagnetic storms.

Sungrazing comet ISON (C/2012 S1) was hyped as a potential 'comet of the century' before its November 2013 perihelion, but it disintegrated as it passed within ~1,200 km of the solar surface. SOHO's coronagraph images showed debris entering perihelion with greatly reduced brightness — a reminder that comet brightness predictions close to the Sun are notoriously unreliable.

The Wow! signal remains the most compelling unexplained candidate for an extraterrestrial radio transmission. Received for exactly 72 seconds on August 15, 1977, at frequency 1420.46 MHz (the 21-cm hydrogen line), its signal strength, narrowband nature, and apparent origin from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius matched the expected properties of an interstellar beacon — but it has never been detected again despite repeated searches.

Neutron star mergers produce r-process elements in quantities now constrained by GW170817 observations: the kilonova ejected ~0.03–0.05 solar masses of r-process material. Extrapolating from merger rates, neutron star mergers alone can account for most of the observed cosmic abundance of gold, platinum, and other heavy r-process elements in the Milky Way.

The Fermi paradox asks: if intelligent life is common in the universe, why don't we see evidence of it? Proposed resolutions include the Rare Earth hypothesis (complex life is extraordinarily rare), the Great Filter (most civilizations destroy themselves before becoming detectable), communication challenges, deliberate silence, and the sheer vastness of the universe making contact statistically unlikely.

The Boomerang Nebula, a planetary nebula in Centaurus, is the coldest naturally occurring region known — about 1 Kelvin, even colder than the cosmic microwave background (2.73 K). This extreme cooling results from gas expanding so rapidly from the central star that it adiabatically cools below the CMB temperature, creating an effective refrigerator around the dying star.

The cosmic distance ladder's fourth rung — surface brightness fluctuations (SBF) — uses the fact that the granularity of the stellar glow in an elliptical galaxy decreases with distance. Nearby galaxies show individual stars that fluctuate point-to-point; distant galaxies appear smoother. SBF gives distances out to ~100 Mpc and is an independent check on Cepheid-calibrated results.

Exoplanet phase curves — full-orbit photometric monitoring of a planetary system — reveal the day-night temperature contrast and thermal emission from the planet without it needing to transit or eclipse. Phase curve observations of hot Jupiters have revealed that their peak temperature is often east of the sub-stellar point, indicating supersonic equatorial jet winds in their atmospheres.

The Galactic Center Gamma-ray Excess — an unexplained excess of gamma-ray emission centered on Sgr A* discovered in Fermi data — has a spectrum and morphology consistent with annihilation of dark matter particles (~40 GeV WIMPs). However, an unresolved population of millisecond pulsars is an equally viable explanation, and the debate remains open.

Titan's atmosphere is dominated by nitrogen (98.4%) with ~1.4% methane. Unlike Earth's water cycle, Titan has a hydrocarbon cycle: methane evaporates from the surface, condenses to form clouds, rains onto mountains, flows in rivers, and collects in polar seas. Photochemistry high in the atmosphere breaks methane down — a mystery since Titan would run out in ~10 million years without a replenishing source.

The Saturn Hexagon is a persistent hexagonal cloud pattern at Saturn's north pole, about 30,000 km across — large enough to fit nearly four Earths inside. It was discovered by Voyager in 1981 and has persisted for decades; Cassini observed it in detail across multiple seasons. Computer models reproduce the hexagon as a standing Rossby wave in the jet stream — a phenomenon not seen on any other planet.

Moons of the outer solar system show a remarkable diversity of geology powered primarily by tidal heating. Miranda (Uranus) has a Verona Rupes cliff 20 km high — the tallest known cliff in the solar system. Ganymede has a unique internally generated magnetic field. Triton (Neptune's large moon) orbits retrograde, suggesting it is a captured Kuiper Belt object, and has active nitrogen geysers.

GJ 504b was one of the first exoplanets directly imaged at near-infrared wavelengths — a massive planet (4–9 Jupiter masses) visible as a magenta point of light orbiting a sun-like star at ~44 AU. The image demonstrates how young, massive planets are self-luminous from their own gravitational contraction heat, making direct imaging possible before they cool.

Phosphine (PH3) was tentatively reported in Venus's atmosphere via JCMT and ALMA observations in 2020 at ~20 ppb. Because phosphine on Earth is only produced biologically or at extreme temperatures/pressures, the claim sparked intense debate. Subsequent reanalyses reduced the signal significance substantially, and the community remains divided on whether any robust phosphine detection exists.

The Bullet Pulsar (B2224+65) is a young pulsar with a proper motion velocity of ~800 km/s relative to surrounding gas, creating a bow shock visible as an H-alpha nebula. It was given a 'guitar nebula' nickname due to its shape. Such high-velocity pulsars received a natal kick from an asymmetric supernova explosion, and measuring their velocities constrains core-collapse supernova physics.

The discovery of pulsars led to a major controversy: because Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a graduate student, made the discovery while Antony Hewish (her supervisor) received the 1974 Nobel Prize for it, her omission became one of the most famous cases in the Nobel Prize's history of controversially ignoring the actual discoverers. Bell Burnell received the Breakthrough Prize and other major awards decades later.

The Coma Cluster, one of the nearest massive galaxy clusters at ~320 million light-years, was the site where Fritz Zwicky in 1933 first inferred the existence of dark matter, noticing that galaxy velocities within the cluster implied far more mass than the visible stars could provide. He called the invisible mass 'dunkle Materie' — dark matter — 40 years before it was widely accepted.

The Perseus Cluster harbors a supermassive black hole (NGC 1275) whose jets have carved enormous X-ray cavities in the hot intracluster gas. In 2003, Chandra discovered that sound waves — ripples in the cluster gas — emanate from the black hole's activity at a frequency 57 octaves below middle C (~10 million years per oscillation), the lowest-pitched known sound waves in the universe.

The Euclid space telescope, launched in July 2023 by ESA, will survey 15,000 square degrees of sky to map the distribution of over 1.5 billion galaxies out to redshift ~2. Its primary science goals are measuring the equation of state of dark energy via weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering, aiming to determine whether dark energy is constant (Λ) or evolving.

The Kuiper Cliff is an unexpected steep drop in the density of Kuiper Belt objects beyond ~50 AU, observed in both large objects and dynamically cold classical KBOs. It may indicate that the outer Kuiper Belt was truncated by the passage of another star in the Sun's birth cluster, or by the influence of a distant undiscovered planet (the hypothetical 'Planet 9').

The Aten, Apollo, and Amor asteroid groups are collectively called near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) and are defined by their orbital relationships to Earth. Aten asteroids have semi-major axes less than 1 AU; Apollo asteroids cross Earth's orbit with semi-major axes greater than 1 AU; Amor asteroids approach but don't cross Earth's orbit. Over 35,000 NEAs are known, with hundreds potentially hazardous.

source.name: NASA Center for Near Earth Object Studies

text: Globular cluster stars are so densely packed near the core that stellar collisions and captures are common, producing exotic objects: blue stragglers (stars that appear younger than the cluster because they accreted mass from a companion), X-ray binaries, and millisecond pulsars. The globular cluster 47 Tucanae alone hosts 23 known millisecond pulsars.

The Boötes Void was discovered in 1981 in a redshift survey of radio galaxies; it measures roughly 250–330 million light-years across and contains only ~60 galaxies where thousands would be expected. Its roughly spherical shape, unusual even among voids, has fueled speculation about its origin — though N-body simulations show such voids can form naturally from gravitational evolution without exotic physics.

The Cosmic Horseshoe (SDSS J1148+1930) is one of the most perfect Einstein rings ever discovered — a near-complete ring formed by gravitational lensing of a blue star-forming galaxy behind a massive foreground elliptical galaxy. The alignment must be within 0.1 arcseconds of perfect for such a near-complete ring to form, and the lensing magnifies the background galaxy ~30 times.

Variable star classification includes eruptive variables (novae, T Tauri stars, flare stars), pulsating variables (Cepheids, RR Lyrae, Mira), rotating variables (spotted stars, rapidly oscillating Ap stars), and cataclysmic variables (novae, dwarf novae, symbiotic stars). The AAVSO International Variable Star Index catalogs over 2 million variable stars.

The Milky Way's bar — a cigar-shaped concentration of stars through its center — was not confirmed observationally until the 1990s and early 2000s, despite being predicted by models. The bar rotates rigidly with a pattern speed of ~30–40 km/s/kpc and may be responsible for driving gas and stars toward the galactic center, fueling star formation there.

The concept of 'habitable zones' has been extended beyond stellar radiation: tidally heated icy moons like Europa and Enceladus might be habitable without receiving significant sunlight (an 'ocean zone' rather than a liquid water zone). This has broadened the search for life beyond stars in the traditional habitable zone and suggests habitability zones in the outer solar system.

The Sagan standard — 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' — is widely applied in the search for extraterrestrial life and biosignatures. When biosignature gases like oxygen, methane, or phosphine are detected in exoplanet atmospheres, astronomers must rigorously rule out all abiotic production mechanisms before claiming biological origin.

Technosignatures are observational signs of technology produced by intelligent beings — distinct from biosignatures which indicate life in general. Examples include radio signals, optical laser pulses, waste heat from megastructures (Dyson spheres), megastructural transits, atmospheric pollution (chlorofluorocarbons), and artificial light on the night side of a planet. NASA funds technosignature research as part of its astrobiology program.

The Galactic habitable zone (GHZ) is the annular region of the Milky Way — roughly 7–9 kiloparsecs from the center — with sufficient metallicity (to form rocky planets) but low enough supernova and AGN radiation and collision rates to allow complex life to survive. The solar system sits near the middle of the GHZ, one reason our location may not be cosmically average.

Exoplanet atmospheres are studied not only through transmission spectroscopy during transit but also through emission spectroscopy during secondary eclipse — when the planet passes behind the star. Subtracting the out-of-eclipse spectrum (star + planet) from the in-eclipse spectrum (star alone) yields the planet's thermal emission spectrum, revealing temperature profiles and chemical abundances on the day side.

Binary black hole mergers detected by LIGO have masses ranging from a few to ~150 solar masses. The event GW190521, detected in 2020, involved an estimated 142 solar mass intermediate-mass black hole remnant — the first observation of an intermediate-mass black hole, filling the long-suspected gap between stellar-mass (~3–100 M_sun) and supermassive (>10^5 M_sun) black holes.

The total solar irradiance (TSI, formerly called the 'solar constant') is the power per unit area from the Sun at Earth's distance (~1361 W/m²). It varies by ~0.1% over the solar cycle. Solar variability contributes negligibly to 21st-century climate change compared to human greenhouse gas emissions, though on longer (Maunder Minimum) timescales it can affect regional climates.

source.name: NASA Solar Radiation and Climate Experiment

text: The 2MASS (Two Micron All Sky Survey) catalogued 470 million stars and 1.6 million galaxies in J, H, and K near-infrared bands between 1997 and 2001. Its all-sky coverage, free of galactic dust obscuration, enabled the first complete census of the Milky Way's structure including its bar and bulge shape, and is still widely used as a photometric reference catalog.

The Chandrasekhar limit's derivation requires both quantum mechanics (Pauli exclusion principle creating electron degeneracy pressure) and special relativity (electrons become relativistic at high density). At this intersection, Chandrasekhar showed the degeneracy pressure is insufficient to halt collapse above ~1.4 solar masses, unifying these two pillars of modern physics through a stellar physics calculation.

Blazars are the most extreme class of active galactic nucleus — quasars whose relativistic jet is pointed almost directly at Earth. The relativistic beaming boosts their apparent brightness and causes rapid variability on timescales of minutes to hours. Blazars are among the most powerful particle accelerators in the universe and are leading sources of high-energy cosmic rays, gamma rays, and neutrinos.

Extragalactic background light (EBL) is the accumulated electromagnetic radiation from all stars and galaxies over cosmic history across UV, optical, and infrared wavelengths. Very high-energy gamma rays from blazars are attenuated when they interact with EBL photons to produce electron-positron pairs, providing an indirect way to measure the EBL and thus the total star formation history of the universe.

The International Space Station provides a unique astronomical perspective: it orbits above most of Earth's atmosphere, enabling continuous UV and X-ray observations. The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) on the ISS has measured the antiproton fraction of cosmic rays with unprecedented precision, finding more antiprotons than standard models predict — potentially a signal of dark matter annihilation.

The discovery that the Milky Way's halo is filled with a hot, diffuse X-ray emitting gas — the Milky Way Circumgalactic Medium (CGM) — has been confirmed by X-ray absorption studies with Chandra and XMM-Newton. The CGM extends hundreds of kiloparsecs, contains more mass in baryons than the stellar disk, and is the reservoir from which the Milky Way draws fuel for future star formation.

Stellar evolution models now include rotation as a key parameter. Rotating stars mix their interiors more efficiently, extending lifetimes on the main sequence, and mass loss through stellar winds is enhanced at high rotation rates. The fastest rotating known star, VFTS 102 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, rotates at ~600 km/s — nearly at its break-up velocity.

The JWST Early Release Science program targeting the SMACS 0723 galaxy cluster produced the deepest infrared image of the universe in terms of integration time vs. source faintness when released in July 2022. The image revealed thousands of galaxies including gravitationally lensed arcs, some of which JWST spectroscopy showed to be among the most distant galaxies then known (z > 10).

Gas giant planets form either by core accretion (a rocky core of ~10 Earth masses accumulates first, then rapidly accretes gas) or by disk instability (gravitational fragmentation of the protoplanetary disk directly forms a gas giant). Core accretion is the dominant mechanism for solar-system-like orbits; disk instability may form massive outer planets and brown dwarf companions.

The zodiacal band — the entire band of zodiacal light extending across the ecliptic — is actually brightest at solar elongations around 30–40° (near the Sun) and fades with increasing angular distance. The gegenschein (antisolar point) is a local secondary maximum. Between them runs the zodiacal band connecting these features, visible from exceptionally dark sites as a complete circle around the ecliptic.

The Cosmic Horseshoe, SDSS J0946+1006 ('the Eye of Sauron'), and the Galaxy Einstein Cross (Q2237+0305) are among the most famous strong gravitational lensing systems. The Einstein Cross consists of a single quasar at z=1.695 lensed into four images by a foreground galaxy at z=0.0394; the image separations are only ~1.8 arcseconds, requiring the quasar and galaxy to be aligned to within hundredths of an arcsecond.

The number of confirmed exoplanets surpassed 5,000 in March 2022, growing from zero confirmed before 1992. As of early 2026, the NASA Exoplanet Archive catalogs over 5,700 confirmed exoplanets from over 4,200 planetary systems. The vast majority (over 3,500) were discovered by the Kepler space telescope via the transit method.

The solar twin 18 Scorpii is the most solar-like star known, with nearly identical temperature, luminosity, mass, and chemical composition to the Sun, but slightly older at ~4.8 billion years. Studying it tells us about the Sun's future evolution; comparing its detailed spectroscopic abundances to the Sun's reveals subtleties in the Sun's chemical history and the possible composition of the Sun's protoplanetary disk.

Gamma-ray pulsars — pulsars detected in gamma rays rather than radio waves — were first discovered in quantity by the Fermi LAT. Over 270 gamma-ray pulsars are now known, including many that were originally identified purely by their pulsed gamma-ray emission with no known radio counterpart, demonstrating that the geometric alignment needed for radio detection is more restrictive than for gamma-ray pulsed emission.

The solar maximum of Solar Cycle 25 (peak ~2025) exceeded predictions — it was more active than solar forecasts suggested, with multiple X-class flares and the largest geomagnetic storm since 2003 occurring in May 2024. Predicting solar activity remains an unsolved problem in solar physics because the solar dynamo that generates the Sun's magnetic field is inherently chaotic.

Near-Earth Object Surveyor (NEO Surveyor), a NASA infrared space telescope, was authorized to launch in 2027 to find at least 90% of all near-Earth asteroids larger than 140 meters within 10 years. It operates in the mid-infrared because asteroid thermal emission in this range allows size determination independent of the asteroid's albedo — a key advantage over optical surveys.

source.name: NASA Center for Near Earth Object Studies

text: The first detection of an extrasolar planet by direct imaging was Epsilon Eridani b, briefly claimed in 1988 but later disputed. The first confirmed directly imaged exoplanet was 2M1207b in 2004, a giant planet orbiting a brown dwarf. The HR 8799 system, imaged in 2008, was the first multi-planet system revealed by direct imaging — showing four giant planets in a single image.

The universe's large-scale structure forms a cosmic web of filaments, sheets, and voids that arose from primordial quantum fluctuations amplified by gravity over 13.8 billion years. The remarkable fact that tiny quantum-scale density variations in the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang seeded the distribution of galaxy superclusters billions of light-years across is one of the most profound confirmations of inflationary cosmology.

Saturn's rings are made predominantly of water ice particles ranging in size from tiny grains to chunks as large as houses. Despite spanning nearly 282,000 kilometers in diameter, the rings are remarkably thin — averaging only about 10 meters thick in most regions.

The Hubble Space Telescope orbits Earth at about 547 kilometers altitude and has made more than 1.5 million observations since its launch in 1990. Its longevity has been enabled by five servicing missions carried out by Space Shuttle astronauts between 1993 and 2009.

Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of active volcanoes continuously reshaping its surface. The intense volcanism is driven by tidal heating from gravitational interactions with Jupiter and its other large moons Europa and Ganymede.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is the thermal afterglow of the Big Bang, filling the entire universe uniformly at a temperature of about 2.725 Kelvin. It was accidentally discovered in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who initially thought the mysterious signal was caused by pigeon droppings on their antenna.

The Oort Cloud is a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system at distances from roughly 2,000 to 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun. It is thought to contain trillions of cometary nuclei and to be the source of long-period comets that occasionally plunge into the inner solar system.

Betelgeuse, the red supergiant star in Orion's shoulder, is so large that if placed at the center of our solar system it would engulf everything out to approximately Jupiter's orbit. It is expected to explode as a supernova sometime within the next 100,000 years.

The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass a white dwarf star can have — approximately 1.4 times the mass of the Sun — before electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support it against gravitational collapse. White dwarfs above this limit collapse into neutron stars or trigger Type Ia supernova explosions.

Mars has the largest volcano in the solar system — Olympus Mons — which stands about 21.9 kilometers above the Martian datum and spans roughly 624 kilometers in diameter at its base. Its enormous size compared to Earth's volcanoes is partly because Mars lacks tectonic plate movement, allowing magma to pile up in one spot for billions of years.

The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter contains millions of rocky bodies, yet its total mass is only about 4% of the Moon's mass — far less than once imagined. Jupiter's gravity prevented these planetesimals from coalescing into a full-sized planet.

Neutron stars pack a mass greater than the Sun into a sphere only about 20 kilometers across, giving them densities so extreme that a teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth. Their interiors may contain exotic states of matter such as quark-gluon plasma that cannot be replicated in any laboratory.

The Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and is now the most distant human-made object, more than 23 billion kilometers from Earth. It continues to transmit scientific data, though its signals take over 22 hours to reach us at the speed of light.

Europa, Jupiter's icy moon, has a global subsurface ocean of liquid water beneath its frozen crust that may contain twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined. The presence of liquid water, an energy source from tidal heating, and likely chemical nutrients makes Europa one of the prime candidates for extraterrestrial life in our solar system.

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way at a distance of about 2.537 million light-years. In approximately 4.5 billion years it will collide and merge with our galaxy in a slow, spectacular gravitational dance that astronomers have already simulated in detail.

Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the International Astronomical Union after the discovery of similarly sized Kuiper Belt Objects, notably Eris. The decision required a new definition of 'planet' that includes clearing the neighborhood around one's orbit — a criterion Pluto fails because it shares the Kuiper Belt with thousands of other objects.

The gravitational wave detections by LIGO in 2015 (first announced in 2016) opened an entirely new observational window on the universe. The signals came from two merging black holes about 1.3 billion light-years away and matched Einstein's general relativistic predictions with extraordinary precision.

A light-year is the distance light travels in one Julian year — approximately 9.461 trillion kilometers or about 63,241 astronomical units. Despite its name, it is a unit of distance, not time, and is commonly used because the distances between stars are so vast that kilometers become impractically large numbers.

The Drake Equation, formulated by astronomer Frank Drake in 1961, provides a probabilistic framework for estimating the number of technologically advanced civilizations in the Milky Way capable of communicating with us. While each of its factors carries enormous uncertainty, the equation remains a valuable organizing tool for the scientific study of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI).

The Sun completes one orbit around the center of the Milky Way galaxy every 225 to 250 million years, a period sometimes called a cosmic year or galactic year. In the approximately 4.6 billion years since the solar system formed, it has completed roughly 20 galactic orbits.

The transit method is currently the most successful technique for finding exoplanets, used by missions like Kepler and TESS. It detects the tiny dimming of a star's light when a planet passes in front of it, and can reveal the planet's orbital period and size relative to its host star.

Neptune was the first planet discovered through mathematical prediction rather than direct observation. In 1846, astronomers Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams independently calculated its probable position based on unexplained perturbations in Uranus's orbit, and Johann Galle confirmed its location within 1 degree of the prediction.

The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is a persistent anticyclonic storm that has been observed for at least 350 years, making it the longest-lived storm known in the solar system. Its diameter has been shrinking over the decades — from about 40,000 km in the 19th century to roughly 14,000 km today — and scientists are uncertain whether it will eventually disappear.

The heliopause marks the outer boundary of the Sun's influence, where the solar wind is finally halted by the pressure of interstellar gas. Voyager 1 crossed this boundary in 2012 at a distance of about 121 astronomical units, officially entering interstellar space.

Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere and the only body beyond Earth known to have stable lakes and rivers of liquid on its surface. Rather than water, Titan's hydrological cycle uses methane and ethane, which exist as liquids in its frigid −179°C environment.

A magnetar is a type of neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field, roughly a trillion times stronger than Earth's. Magnetars occasionally release colossal bursts of gamma rays and X-rays; a magnetar flare in 2004 (from SGR 1806-20) was so energetic it briefly ionized Earth's upper atmosphere despite being 50,000 light-years away.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the outer solar system extending from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU to about 50 AU, populated by icy bodies including Pluto, Eris, Makemake, and Haumea. It is analogous to the asteroid belt but is about 20 times as wide and 20 to 200 times as massive.

Brown dwarfs occupy the mass gap between the heaviest gas giant planets (about 13 Jupiter masses) and the lightest hydrogen-burning stars (about 80 Jupiter masses). They shine feebly from the heat of formation and, if massive enough, from brief deuterium fusion, but never ignite sustained hydrogen fusion.

The radial velocity (Doppler wobble) method for detecting exoplanets measures the tiny back-and-forth motion of a star caused by the gravitational tug of an orbiting planet. The first confirmed exoplanet around a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was discovered this way in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, who later shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Venus rotates on its axis so slowly that a Venusian day (243 Earth days) is longer than a Venusian year (225 Earth days). Additionally, Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets — a retrograde spin — so on Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

Cepheid variable stars pulsate with a period directly related to their intrinsic luminosity, making them invaluable 'standard candles' for measuring cosmic distances. Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered this period-luminosity relationship in 1908 by studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a discovery that eventually revealed the true scale of the universe.

Uranus rotates on its side with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees — essentially rolling around the Sun rather than spinning upright like most planets. This extreme tilt causes each hemisphere to experience 42-year-long periods of continuous sunlight or total darkness as Uranus orbits the Sun.

The Milky Way galaxy contains an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars and is classified as a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years in diameter. Our solar system is located about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center in one of the spiral arms called the Orion Arm.

Solar flares are sudden intense bursts of energy from the Sun's surface that release radiation across the entire electromagnetic spectrum in seconds to minutes. The most powerful solar flare ever recorded, the Carrington Event of 1859, caused auroras visible as far south as Cuba and burned out telegraph systems across North America and Europe.

The observable universe spans approximately 93 billion light-years in diameter, even though the universe is only about 13.8 billion years old. This seeming paradox arises because space itself has been expanding since the Big Bang, carrying distant galaxies farther away faster than their light can travel toward us.

Quasars (quasi-stellar objects) are the extremely luminous active cores of distant galaxies powered by supermassive black holes consuming matter at enormous rates. The most luminous quasars outshine their entire host galaxies by factors of thousands and can be observed from billions of light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched on December 25, 2021, observes primarily in infrared light and is positioned at the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. Its primary mirror is 6.5 meters across and consists of 18 gold-plated beryllium hexagonal segments.

The Fermi paradox asks why, given the high probability that intelligent extraterrestrial civilizations exist in the vast universe, we have no confirmed contact with any of them. Physicist Enrico Fermi reportedly asked 'Where is everybody?' during a 1950 lunch conversation, spawning decades of speculation about the nature of intelligent life in the cosmos.

Pulsars are rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles, sweeping through space like cosmic lighthouses. The first pulsar was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish; the signal was so regular that it was initially nicknamed LGM-1 for 'Little Green Men.'

Mercury has almost no atmosphere to trap heat, causing its surface to swing between extreme temperatures — reaching 430°C on the sunlit side and plunging to −180°C on the night side. Despite being the closest planet to the Sun, Mercury is not the hottest planet; Venus holds that distinction due to its thick, heat-trapping carbon dioxide atmosphere.

Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe's total energy content but has never been directly detected; its existence is inferred from its gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation, and the large-scale structure of the universe. Galaxy rotation curves — which stay flat instead of declining with distance from the galactic center — provide some of the most compelling indirect evidence for dark matter.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile consists of 66 high-precision antennas that work together as an interferometer to study cold, dark objects invisible to optical telescopes, such as protoplanetary disks and the earliest galaxies. It produced the first resolved image of a protoplanetary disk around a young star (HL Tauri) in 2014, revealing intricate ring and gap structures.

The cosmic distance ladder is a succession of methods astronomers use to measure increasingly large distances in the universe, with each rung calibrated by the one below it. Methods include parallax for nearby stars, Cepheid variables for nearby galaxies, and Type Ia supernovae for distances reaching billions of light-years.

The Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram plots stars by their luminosity versus their surface temperature, revealing that most stars cluster along a band called the main sequence. This diagram is a fundamental tool in stellar astrophysics, showing the evolutionary stages of stars and the relationships between their observable properties.

The Cassini spacecraft spent 13 years orbiting Saturn before plunging into its atmosphere in 2017, transmitting data right up to the end. Its discoveries include geysers of water vapor on Enceladus, vast hydrocarbon lakes on Titan, and the remarkable complexity of Saturn's ring system including previously unknown ring structures.

An astronomical unit (AU) is defined as exactly 149,597,870.7 kilometers — the mean distance from Earth to the Sun as formalized by the IAU in 2012. It serves as a convenient yardstick for measuring distances within the solar system and is used widely in planetary science.

The New Horizons mission made the first-ever close flyby of Pluto on July 14, 2015, revealing a world of surprising geological complexity including nitrogen ice plains (informally named Tombaugh Regio), towering water ice mountains, and a tenuous nitrogen atmosphere. It then flew past the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth (2014 MU69) in 2019, revealing a bilobate contact binary formed by gentle collision.

The concept of a black hole event horizon — the boundary of no return from which not even light can escape — was first mathematically described by Karl Schwarzschild in 1916, just months after Einstein published his general theory of relativity. The radius of this boundary is called the Schwarzschild radius and is directly proportional to the black hole's mass.

The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) mapped the CMB temperature fluctuations across the full sky with unprecedented precision between 2001 and 2010. Its data established the standard cosmological model — a flat universe composed of approximately 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, and 68% dark energy.

Stellar nucleosynthesis is the process by which stars forge heavy elements from lighter ones through nuclear fusion in their cores. All elements heavier than helium — including the carbon in your body and the iron in your blood — were synthesized inside stars and distributed into space when those stars died.

The Gaia space observatory, launched by ESA in 2013, is mapping the positions, distances, and motions of more than 1.5 billion stars in the Milky Way with extraordinary precision. Its data releases have revolutionized stellar cartography and revealed dozens of previously unknown stellar streams from ancient galaxy mergers absorbed by our own galaxy.

A parsec — the standard unit of distance used by professional astronomers — equals approximately 3.26 light-years or about 3.086 × 10^13 kilometers. It is defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond, making it directly related to the parallax method of distance measurement.

Mars's two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, are likely captured asteroids or remnants of a giant impact. Phobos orbits so close to Mars — just 6,000 km above the surface — that tidal forces are slowly spiraling it inward; within about 50 million years it will either break apart into a ring or crash into the Martian surface.

The interstellar medium (ISM) — the gas and dust that fills the space between stars — is not empty: it contains about one atom per cubic centimeter on average, compared to the roughly 10^19 atoms per cubic centimeter in Earth's atmosphere at sea level. Despite its extreme tenuousness the ISM is the raw material from which new stars and planets form.

Globular clusters are tightly packed spherical collections of hundreds of thousands to millions of very old stars, dating back to the early universe. The Milky Way hosts about 150 known globular clusters, with Omega Centauri being the largest, containing roughly 10 million stars and possibly being the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy.

The precession of Earth's rotational axis traces a slow wobble with a period of approximately 26,000 years, caused primarily by the gravitational torque of the Moon and Sun on Earth's equatorial bulge. This precession means that Polaris has not always been the North Star — about 13,000 years ago, Vega was the pole star, and it will be again in another 13,000 years.

The Virgo Supercluster — also called Laniakea — is a massive supercluster of galaxies spanning about 520 million light-years and containing the Milky Way, the Andromeda Galaxy, and thousands of other galaxies. Astronomers mapped its full extent in 2014 using galaxy velocity flows converging toward the 'Great Attractor' at its center.

The first image of a black hole's shadow — the supermassive black hole M87* at the center of galaxy Messier 87 — was captured by the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration and published in April 2019. The image required a planet-spanning network of synchronized radio telescopes operating as a virtual Earth-sized dish.

Enceladus, Saturn's sixth-largest moon, actively vents plumes of water vapor, ice, and organic molecules from a subsurface ocean through cracks in its south polar ice shell known as 'tiger stripes.' The Cassini spacecraft flew through these plumes and confirmed the presence of molecular hydrogen, a potential chemical energy source for life.

The cosmic inflation hypothesis proposes that the universe underwent an exponential expansion during the first 10^-36 to 10^-32 seconds after the Big Bang, growing by a factor of at least 10^26. Inflation explains why the CMB is nearly uniform across the sky and why the universe's geometry appears spatially flat.

Variable stars are stars whose brightness changes over time due to intrinsic physical processes such as pulsation, eruption, or binary eclipses. The American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO) maintains a database of observations by amateur and professional astronomers covering millions of observations over more than a century.

The rings of Uranus were the first planetary ring system to be discovered after Saturn's, found in 1977 when Uranus occulted a background star and astronomers noticed the star dimmed briefly before and after it was blocked by the planet itself. Neptune's rings were similarly found through stellar occultations before Voyager 2's flyby confirmed them.

The Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way has a mass of about 4 million solar masses. The Event Horizon Telescope published the first image of Sgr A* in May 2022, capturing its glowing ring of hot gas around a dark central shadow.

The Leonid meteor shower, which originates from debris shed by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, can produce meteor storms under certain conditions — rates of tens of thousands of meteors per hour — when Earth passes through particularly dense debris trails. Major storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, and 1999–2002.

Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are intense millisecond-duration radio pulses of unknown origin, first detected in 2007 in archival data from the Parkes radio telescope. Many FRBs originate from galaxies billions of light-years away and release as much energy in a millisecond as the Sun emits over thousands of years; some repeat, pointing to a non-destructive mechanism such as magnetar flares.

The Sun's core temperature reaches approximately 15 million degrees Celsius, hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium through the proton-proton chain, releasing the energy that powers the Sun. Each second, the Sun converts about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, losing about 4 million tons of mass as pure energy via E=mc².

The zodiacal light is a faint triangular glow visible in a dark sky along the ecliptic shortly after sunset or before sunrise, caused by sunlight scattering off interplanetary dust grains concentrated in the plane of the solar system. Data from the Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, suggested Venus may be the primary source of much of this dust.

Tidal locking occurs when one body's rotation period synchronizes with its orbital period due to gravitational forces, causing the same face to permanently point toward the central body. Earth's Moon is tidally locked to Earth, which is why we always see the same side of the Moon — the far side remained entirely unseen until Luna 3 photographed it in 1959.

The cosmic neutrino background (CνB) is a relic sea of neutrinos produced about one second after the Big Bang, analogous to the CMB but from an even earlier epoch. These neutrinos pervade every cubic centimeter of the universe at an average density of about 336 per cubic centimeter but are extraordinarily difficult to detect due to their nearly zero interaction cross-section with matter.

Radio telescopes detect radio waves from cosmic sources and can operate in daylight and through clouds — conditions that would ruin optical observations. The world's largest single-dish radio telescope is the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) in China, which became operational in 2016 and has discovered hundreds of new pulsars.

Halley's Comet, one of the most famous short-period comets, returns to the inner solar system approximately every 75 years and has been recorded by astronomers for at least 2,000 years. Its next perihelion passage — closest approach to the Sun — is expected in July 2061.

Gravitational lensing occurs when a massive object bends the path of light passing near it, acting as a natural cosmic telescope that can magnify and distort images of background galaxies and quasars. The first confirmed gravitational lens was discovered in 1979 (the Twin Quasar Q0957+561), and Einstein rings — perfect circular arcs around lensing galaxies — have since been found in large numbers.

The solar corona — the Sun's outermost layer visible as a glowing halo during total solar eclipses — reaches temperatures of one to three million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the solar surface at about 5,500°C. The coronal heating problem — why the corona is so much hotter than the surface below it — remains one of the outstanding unsolved problems in solar physics.

Stellar parallax is the apparent shift in a nearby star's position against the background of distant stars as Earth orbits the Sun. The first successful stellar parallax measurement was made by Friedrich Bessel in 1838 for the star 61 Cygni, yielding a distance of about 11.4 light-years — very close to the modern value of 11.43 light-years.

The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009 and retired in 2018, confirmed more than 2,600 exoplanets by monitoring the brightness of roughly 150,000 stars simultaneously for transit signals. Its data revolutionized our understanding of planetary system demographics, establishing that small rocky planets are extremely common around sun-like stars.

The Local Group is the gravitationally bound collection of over 50 galaxies that includes the Milky Way and Andromeda as its two dominant members. Most Local Group galaxies are small dwarf galaxies orbiting the two giants, and the whole group spans about 10 million light-years.

Charon, Pluto's largest moon, is so big relative to Pluto — about half Pluto's diameter — that the two bodies orbit their common center of mass (barycenter) which lies outside Pluto itself. This makes Pluto-Charon the closest thing to a true binary dwarf planet system in our solar system.

The Big Rip is a hypothetical cosmological model in which the accelerating expansion of the universe eventually overcomes all other forces — gravity, electromagnetism, and even the strong nuclear force — tearing apart galaxies, stars, planets, atoms, and subatomic particles in a finite time. It depends on the nature of dark energy, which remains unknown.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are the compact, extremely luminous central regions of some galaxies powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes. The different observational appearances of AGN — quasars, Seyfert galaxies, blazars, radio galaxies — are partly explained by the unified model, which attributes differences to the angle at which we view the same basic structure.

The Arecibo Message, transmitted in 1974 toward the globular cluster M13, was a binary-encoded radio signal containing information about Earth's location, human biology, and our number system. It was sent not out of expectation of a reply but as a demonstration of humanity's radio communications technology.

The Moon's orbital distance is not constant: it is slowly receding from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters per year due to tidal interactions. Billions of years ago the Moon was much closer to Earth, producing enormous tides, and Earth's day was significantly shorter — around 6 hours long.

Planetary nebulae — colorful, shell-like structures surrounding dying Sun-like stars — have nothing to do with planets; they were named by William Herschel in the 18th century because they resembled the fuzzy disc of Uranus through his telescope. They form when a red giant sheds its outer layers, which are then ionized and lit up by the hot white dwarf remnant at the center.

The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles — mostly electrons and protons — flowing outward from the Sun at speeds of 400 to 800 kilometers per second. It shapes the magnetospheres of planets, blows back comet tails, and, when it interacts with Earth's magnetic field, produces the auroras borealis and australis.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), which began collecting data in 2000, mapped more than a third of the sky in multiple wavelengths, imaging hundreds of millions of galaxies and spectra for millions of stars. Its datasets have enabled thousands of scientific papers and established the large-scale structure of the nearby universe in unparalleled detail.

Stellar mass black holes form when massive stars (greater than roughly 20 solar masses) exhaust their nuclear fuel and undergo gravitational collapse, often accompanied by a core-collapse supernova. Binary systems containing a stellar-mass black hole actively accreting from a companion star — called X-ray binaries — are among the brightest X-ray sources in the sky.

The Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is an interferometric radio telescope facility consisting of 27 dish antennas each 25 meters in diameter arranged in a Y-shaped configuration. When fully extended, its maximum baseline is 36 kilometers, giving it an angular resolution comparable to optical telescopes.

Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke into 21 fragments under Jupiter's tidal forces and then collided with Jupiter in July 1994, producing impact scars larger than Earth visible for months. It was the first direct observation of two solar system bodies colliding and provided invaluable insights into Jupiter's atmosphere and the impact threat to planets.

The Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) in Chile has made high-resolution measurements of the CMB that complement those of Planck, probing smaller angular scales where the signatures of secondary processes like gravitational lensing and the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect are important. ACT results have contributed to measurements of the Hubble constant that are in tension with early-universe predictions.

The mass-energy equivalence expressed in Einstein's equation E=mc² explains why nuclear reactions release such enormous energy: even tiny amounts of mass correspond to vast amounts of energy when multiplied by the square of the speed of light (approximately 9×10^16 m²/s²). The nuclear fusion in the Sun's core converts only 0.7% of hydrogen mass into energy, yet this small fraction powers the Sun for billions of years.

The cosmic abundance of elements shows that hydrogen accounts for about 75% of ordinary baryonic matter by mass in the universe, helium makes up about 24%, and all heavier elements combined constitute less than 2%. This primordial mix is the legacy of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, which occurred in the first three minutes after the Big Bang.

Mars has a very thin atmosphere — less than 1% of Earth's sea-level pressure — composed mostly of carbon dioxide. Despite this, Mars experiences massive dust storms that can envelop the entire planet and last for months, dramatically reducing sunlight reaching the surface and posing challenges for solar-powered Mars rovers.

Synchrotron radiation is emitted when relativistic electrons spiral around magnetic field lines and is produced in many extreme astrophysical environments, including the jets of active galaxies and the remnants of supernovae. The Crab Nebula, the remnant of a supernova seen in 1054 AD, is a powerful synchrotron emitter whose glow is powered by the rapidly spinning pulsar at its center.

The Geminid meteor shower, peaking each December around the 13th-14th, is unique among major annual showers in that it originates from an asteroid — 3200 Phaethon — rather than a comet. It is one of the most prolific showers of the year, producing up to 120 multicolored meteors per hour at its peak under ideal conditions.

The surface of the Sun is called the photosphere, a turbulent layer about 500 km thick at approximately 5,500°C where convection cells called granules — each roughly the size of Texas — constantly rise and fall with a lifetime of about 8 to 20 minutes. Above the photosphere lies the chromosphere, visible as a red rim during total solar eclipses, and beyond it the million-degree corona.

The Magellanic Clouds — the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds — are irregular dwarf galaxies visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere, located about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away respectively. They are gravitationally interacting with the Milky Way and with each other, and are gradually being tidally stripped of stars and gas that form a structure called the Magellanic Stream.

Hot Jupiters are a class of gas giant exoplanets with orbital periods of just a few days, orbiting far closer to their host stars than Mercury does to our Sun. Their discovery in 1995 was completely unexpected and challenged prevailing planet formation models; they are now understood to have formed farther out and migrated inward due to interactions with the protoplanetary disk.

Gravitational microlensing occurs when a massive object passes in front of a more distant star, briefly magnifying its light as a gravitational lens. This technique can reveal free-floating planets (rogue planets with no host star), exoplanets in wide orbits, and other compact objects that are otherwise invisible, making it a unique complement to transit and radial velocity surveys.

The heliosphere — the vast bubble of space dominated by the Sun's magnetic field and solar wind — extends well beyond Neptune, shielding the inner solar system from much of the galactic cosmic radiation. The shape of the heliosphere is not perfectly spherical but resembles a comet with a tail pointing away from the direction of the Sun's motion through the galaxy.

The Planck satellite, operated by ESA from 2009 to 2013, produced the most detailed full-sky maps of the CMB ever made, measuring temperature fluctuations at the level of a few millionths of a Kelvin. Its results refined the age of the universe (13.813 ± 0.038 billion years) and the densities of dark matter, dark energy, and ordinary matter with unprecedented precision.

The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT), under construction at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, will use seven 8.4-meter primary mirror segments arranged to form an effective 25.4-meter aperture when complete. It will enable direct imaging and spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres and probe the earliest stars and galaxies.

Spectroscopy — the analysis of light broken into its component wavelengths — is the primary tool by which astronomers determine the chemical composition, temperature, density, motion, and magnetic fields of astronomical objects. Fraunhofer lines, the dark absorption lines in the solar spectrum first catalogued by Joseph von Fraunhofer in 1814, provided the first evidence that the Sun contains the same elements found on Earth.

The Rubin Observatory (formerly LSST), nearing first light at Cerro Pachón in Chile, will use a 3.2-gigapixel camera to repeatedly image the entire southern sky every few nights for ten years. Its survey is expected to discover millions of new transients including supernovae, near-Earth asteroids, and variable stars, transforming our ability to study the time-varying universe.

The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) being built by ESO on Cerro Armazones in Chile will have a primary mirror 39 meters across — the largest optical telescope ever constructed. Its adaptive optics system will correct for atmospheric turbulence in real time using a laser guide star and a secondary mirror that can deform its shape 1,000 times per second.

The Milky Way's central bar — a elongated region of older stars stretching across the galactic center — is estimated to span about 27,000 light-years end to end. Barred spiral galaxies like ours account for about two-thirds of all spiral galaxies, and the bar plays an important role in channeling gas toward the central regions where star formation can be triggered.

The Voyager Golden Records, carried aboard both Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977, are gold-plated copper discs containing sounds and images of Earth intended as a time capsule and greeting to any interstellar civilization that might recover them. They include music from around the world, greetings in 55 languages, and diagrams explaining how to play the record.

Gravitational waves from the neutron star merger GW170817, detected in 2017, were accompanied by a gamma-ray burst detected 1.7 seconds later — confirming that short gamma-ray bursts are produced by neutron star mergers. Subsequent observations across the electromagnetic spectrum revealed a kilonova, providing direct evidence that heavy r-process elements like gold and platinum are forged in neutron star collisions.

Astroseismology (also called stellar seismology) studies oscillations — essentially starquakes — in stellar interiors to probe conditions that are otherwise inaccessible to direct observation. The Kepler and TESS missions have measured oscillations in tens of thousands of stars, enabling precise measurements of stellar ages, masses, and internal rotation profiles.

The interstellar object 1I/'Oumuamua, discovered in 2017, was the first confirmed object from another star system to visit our solar system. Its extreme elongated shape (estimated aspect ratio of at least 5:1), non-gravitational acceleration, and total lack of observable cometary outgassing made it deeply puzzling, and its origin and nature remain debated.

Borisov (2I/Borisov), discovered in 2019, is the second confirmed interstellar object and the first interstellar comet — unlike 'Oumuamua it displayed a clear cometary coma and tail as it passed through the inner solar system. Its composition appeared broadly similar to solar system comets, suggesting that the same icy building blocks of planets form around other stars.

The Hubble tension refers to the discrepancy between two independent measurements of the Hubble constant — the rate at which the universe is expanding. Early-universe measurements from the CMB (Planck) give about 67 km/s/Mpc, while late-universe measurements from Cepheid-calibrated supernovae give about 73 km/s/Mpc, a disagreement now exceeding 5 sigma that may point to new physics.

The Crab Pulsar, the rapidly spinning neutron star at the heart of the Crab Nebula, rotates 30.2 times per second and emits pulses across the entire electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays. It was formed in the supernova of 1054 AD, recorded by Chinese and Arab astronomers as a 'guest star' bright enough to be visible in daylight for 23 days.

Adaptive optics systems on ground-based telescopes use deformable mirrors controlled by computers to correct in real time for the blurring effect of atmospheric turbulence. Modern AO systems can achieve angular resolutions matching or exceeding the Hubble Space Telescope for targets bright enough or close enough to natural guide stars.

Super-Earths are exoplanets with masses between those of Earth and Neptune (roughly 1 to 10 Earth masses) with no solar system analogue. They are the most common type of planet found by Kepler around sun-like stars; whether they are rocky super-sized Earths or mini ice giants with thick volatile envelopes depends heavily on their location relative to the snow line during formation.

Cosmic rays are high-energy charged particles — mostly protons and atomic nuclei — that bombard Earth's upper atmosphere from all directions at nearly the speed of light. The most energetic cosmic rays detected (ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, or UHECRs) have energies exceeding 10^20 eV — equivalent to a baseball pitched at 60 mph packed into a single subatomic particle — and their sources remain mysterious.

The Spitzer Space Telescope, launched in 2003 and decommissioned in 2020, observed the universe in infrared from 3 to 180 microns and revealed warm dust, cool stars, and distant galaxies invisible to optical telescopes. Among its many discoveries, it detected for the first time the thermal emission spectrum of an exoplanet's atmosphere (HD 209458b) in 2005.

The habitable zone (or Goldilocks zone) around a star is the range of orbital distances at which liquid water could theoretically exist on a rocky planet's surface, given sufficient atmospheric pressure. Its boundaries depend not only on stellar luminosity but also on planetary atmospheric composition and the greenhouse effect, making precise habitability assessments complex.

The dwarf planet Eris, discovered in 2005 and the most distant known object in the solar system at the time, is only slightly smaller than Pluto but about 27% more massive. Its discovery directly prompted the IAU debate that resulted in Pluto's reclassification, since astronomers were unwilling to call Eris — and potentially dozens of similar objects — planets.

Stellar populations are classified by the astronomers Walter Baade as Population I (younger, metal-rich stars found in galactic discs) and Population II (older, metal-poor stars found in galactic bulges and halos). A hypothetical Population III — the first generation of stars formed entirely from hydrogen and helium after the Big Bang with no metals — has never been directly detected but is thought to have been massive and short-lived.

The Schwarzschild metric — the exact solution to Einstein's field equations for the spacetime around a non-rotating, spherically symmetric mass — predicts that time passes more slowly in stronger gravitational fields, an effect called gravitational time dilation. GPS satellites must account for this effect (as well as special relativistic time dilation from their orbital velocity) or their clocks would drift by about 38 microseconds per day, causing navigation errors accumulating to kilometers.

Infrared astronomy is essential for studying objects obscured by dust, including star-forming regions, galactic centres, and the most distant galaxies whose visible light has been redshifted into the infrared. The JWST can see light emitted when the universe was less than 400 million years old, directly capturing the era of cosmic reionisation when the first galaxies began to illuminate the universe.

The Milky Way's supermassive black hole Sgr A* was first identified as an unusual radio source in 1974 by Bruce Balick and Robert Brown. Decades of monitoring by Andrea Ghez (UCLA) and Reinhard Genzel (Max Planck) tracked the orbits of stars at the galactic centre — especially the star S2 on a 16-year orbit — earning them the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The cosmic web's voids — vast underdense regions tens to hundreds of millions of light-years across — contain almost no galaxies but account for most of the universe's volume. Galaxies and their clusters lie along the filaments and sheets that surround these voids like a cosmic sponge, forming the largest structures in the observable universe.

The Opportunity Mars rover, launched in 2003, was designed for a 90-day mission but operated for almost 15 years before a global dust storm in 2018 silenced it. During its 45.16-kilometer traverse — the farthest driven by any off-Earth vehicle at the time — it confirmed that Mars once had liquid water environments potentially habitable for microbial life.

Comet tails always point away from the Sun regardless of the direction of the comet's travel, because they are driven by solar radiation pressure and the solar wind rather than by the comet's motion. A comet actually has two distinct tails: a straight bluish ion tail and a curved white dust tail.

Exomoons — moons orbiting planets in other solar systems — have been tentatively identified in a few cases using transit timing variations and other indirect methods, but none has been definitively confirmed as of 2025. Their detection requires measurements of extraordinary precision because their photometric signal is far smaller than that of the host planet's transit.

Io's volcanoes include some of the most powerful in the solar system — the volcano Loki Patera is a lava lake roughly the size of Lake Ontario that periodically overturns its crust every 400 to 600 days. The New Horizons spacecraft photographed a plume from Tvashtar volcano rising 330 kilometers above Io's surface during its 2007 flyby.

The Palomar-Leiden Survey of the 1960s–70s was one of the first systematic searches for asteroids, discovering thousands of new objects. Today the Catalina Sky Survey, Pan-STARRS, and other automated programs discover hundreds of thousands of new solar system bodies each year, catalogued in the Minor Planet Center's ever-growing database.

The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect describes the spectral distortion of CMB photons when they scatter off the hot electrons in the intracluster medium of galaxy clusters. It provides a powerful method to discover and characterize galaxy clusters independent of their redshift, because the SZ signal does not diminish with distance in the same way that optical brightness does.

The Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA) population includes over 33,000 known objects as of 2025, with roughly 2,200 classified as Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs) based on their size and proximity to Earth's orbit. NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission in 2022 deliberately impacted the moonlet Dimorphos and successfully changed its orbit, demonstrating kinetic impactor planetary defense technology for the first time.

White dwarfs are stellar remnants left over after Sun-like stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Despite being approximately Earth-sized, a white dwarf retains most of the star's original mass, making it extraordinarily dense; it slowly cools over billions of years, eventually becoming a theoretical 'black dwarf' — though the universe is not yet old enough for any black dwarfs to exist.

Transit spectroscopy allows astronomers to characterize exoplanet atmospheres by comparing the star's spectrum when the planet transits in front of it to when it does not. Molecules in the exoplanet's atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths of starlight as it passes through, and JWST has detected carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor in exoplanet atmospheres this way.

Sagittarius B2, a giant molecular cloud near the galactic centre, contains a rich inventory of complex organic molecules including ethanol, glycolaldehyde (a simple sugar), and even amino acid precursors detected by radio spectroscopy. Such molecules, seeded into proto-stellar nebulae, support the idea that the chemical building blocks of life are widely distributed throughout the galaxy.

The T Tauri phase is an early stage of stellar evolution for low-mass stars before they reach the main sequence, characterised by strong solar winds, intense X-ray emission, and irregular variability. T Tauri stars are surrounded by protoplanetary disks that are sculpted by stellar winds and radiation while planets are forming.

The solar system's formation began about 4.6 billion years ago when a molecular cloud collapsed, likely triggered by a nearby supernova shock wave. The Sun formed at the centre from most of the cloud's material, while the remaining disk of gas and dust — the solar nebula — gradually coagulated into planets, moons, asteroids, and comets.

The Milky Way is thought to have at least two major satellite galaxies — the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds — and a retinue of roughly 50 smaller dwarf galaxies orbiting at various distances. Many of these satellites were discovered only in the past two decades through deep photometric surveys like SDSS that could detect their sparse stellar populations.

Reionisation was the cosmological epoch, roughly 200 million to 1 billion years after the Big Bang, when the first stars and galaxies emitted enough ultraviolet radiation to ionise the neutral hydrogen that had filled the universe since recombination. JWST is directly observing galaxies from this era for the first time, finding them to be surprisingly bright and numerous.

Stellar occultations — events in which a solar system body passes in front of a distant star — provide precise size and shape measurements and can reveal ring systems, thin atmospheres, and surface features. The rings of Pluto's atmosphere thickness were constrained by occultation observations, and the rings of Uranus and Neptune were discovered this way.

The Didymos-Dimorphos binary asteroid system was the target of the DART mission. After DART's impact in September 2022, subsequent observations showed that Dimorphos's orbital period around Didymos shortened by 33 minutes — far more than the minimum 73 seconds needed to declare the mission a success — indicating that the ejecta momentum enhancement played a major role.

Blazars are a subclass of active galactic nuclei where the jet is pointed almost directly toward Earth, making them the most luminous persistent sources in the universe at some wavelengths. The IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica has detected high-energy neutrinos coinciding in direction with flaring blazars, suggesting these objects are also cosmic ray accelerators.

The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite, launched in 1989, made two landmark discoveries: it confirmed that the CMB has a near-perfect blackbody spectrum and detected its tiny temperature anisotropies at the level of one part in 100,000. The principal investigators John Mather and George Smoot were awarded the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for these results.

Trojan asteroids share a planet's orbit around the Sun, clustering at the gravitationally stable L4 and L5 Lagrange points located 60 degrees ahead and behind the planet. Jupiter has the largest known trojan population — over 12,000 confirmed objects — and NASA's Lucy mission, launched in 2021, is visiting six Jovian trojans to study these pristine relics of solar system formation.

The Jeans mass is the minimum mass a region of gas must have for gravity to overcome thermal pressure and collapse to form a star. It depends on the gas temperature and density — cold, dense molecular clouds fragment into clumps of roughly the Jeans mass, with each clump potentially forming one or a few stars.

The TRAPPIST-1 system, announced in full in 2017, hosts seven rocky planets orbiting an ultracool red dwarf star 40 light-years away — with three planets firmly in the habitable zone. The planets have sizes and masses comparable to Earth and are packed so tightly that gravitational interactions cause each planet to exert measurable tidal effects on its neighbours.

Insolation is the amount of solar radiation reaching a planetary surface per unit area, and it varies with both orbital distance and the planet's axial tilt. For Earth, variations in insolation caused by periodic changes in orbital eccentricity, axial tilt, and precession — the Milankovitch cycles — are believed to drive the ice ages over timescales of tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of years.

The Square Kilometre Array (SKA), currently under construction in South Africa and Australia, will be the world's largest radio telescope when complete, with a collecting area of about one square kilometre. It will be sensitive enough to detect an airport radar on a planet 50 light-years away and will conduct transformational surveys of pulsars, hydrogen in the early universe, and tests of fundamental physics.

The luminosity of main-sequence stars scales approximately as the fourth power of their mass (L ∝ M^4), meaning stars twice as massive as the Sun are roughly 16 times more luminous. This relationship means that massive stars exhaust their nuclear fuel vastly faster than lower-mass stars — a 40-solar-mass star may live only a few million years, while a 0.1-solar-mass red dwarf can burn for trillions of years.

Solar wind interaction with a comet creates a bow shock upstream of the comet's nucleus and generates an induced magnetosphere even though comets have no intrinsic magnetic field. The ESA Rosetta mission, which orbited Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko from 2014 to 2016, made in-situ measurements of this plasma environment and monitored the comet's activity through its perihelion passage.

The detection of phosphine in Venus's atmosphere announced in 2020, and the subsequent intense scientific controversy, highlighted the difficulty of confidently attributing atmospheric chemical anomalies to biological processes. Even though the original phosphine claim became disputed due to data processing issues, it sparked renewed interest in Venus atmospheric habitability and the need for in-situ measurements.

The Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy (Sgr dSph) is currently being cannibalized by the Milky Way, with tidal streams of stars from it wrapping multiple times around our galaxy. Many of the stars in the Milky Way's thick disc and halo may have originally been members of dwarf galaxies that were accreted over billions of years in this same way.

The auroral zones on Jupiter and Saturn are more energetically powerful than Earth's auroras and are driven by different mechanisms. Jupiter's auroras are partly powered by the volcanic activity of Io — sulfur and oxygen ions from Io's plumes are picked up by Jupiter's rotating magnetosphere and accelerated along field lines into the atmosphere.

The spectral classification of stars (O, B, A, F, G, K, M — traditionally remembered with 'Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy Kiss Me') sorts stars from hottest blue-white (O-type, >30,000 K) to coolest red (M-type, 2,400–3,700 K). The Sun is a G2V star, meaning it is a yellow-white main-sequence star with a surface temperature of about 5,778 K.

Rogue planets (or free-floating planets) are planet-mass objects that were ejected from their home solar systems during dynamical interactions and now drift through interstellar space with no host star. Gravitational microlensing surveys suggest they may be extremely numerous — possibly exceeding the number of stars in the galaxy — making them a significant but largely undetected component of the Milky Way.

The InSight Mars lander, operating from 2018 to 2022, used a seismometer to detect hundreds of Marsquakes, revealing that Mars has a thin crust, a partially liquid mantle, and a surprisingly large liquid iron core. These were the first seismic measurements of the interior of another planet.

The emission spectrum of a nebula reveals which elements are present: the distinctive red glow of most emission nebulae comes from hydrogen alpha emission at 656 nm, while forbidden lines of ionised oxygen at 495 and 501 nm produce the vivid green-blue hues seen in many Hubble images. 'Forbidden' transitions are so slow they can only occur in the extremely low densities of interstellar space.

The Chandrasekhar-Weizsäcker-Bethe cycle (CNO cycle) is an alternative to the proton-proton chain as a mechanism for hydrogen fusion in stars, using carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen as catalysts. It becomes the dominant energy source in stars more massive than about 1.3 solar masses, where the higher core temperatures needed to overcome the higher Coulomb barrier are achieved.

The Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, has made the closest approaches to the Sun ever achieved by a spacecraft, reaching within about 6.1 million kilometres of the solar surface. It has directly sampled the solar corona and measured the solar wind near its origin, finding evidence for localised 'switchbacks' — reversals in the magnetic field — that may contribute to solar wind acceleration.

The Boötes Void is one of the largest known voids in the universe, a roughly spherical underdense region spanning approximately 250 million light-years. Discovered in 1981, it was initially so astonishing to observers that astronomer Robert Kirshner described the finding as discovering 'a hole in the universe.'

The Chandra X-ray Observatory, launched in 1999, is the world's most powerful X-ray telescope and has revealed the high-energy universe in unprecedented detail. Its discoveries include detailed maps of supernova remnants, jets from black holes spanning millions of light-years, and X-ray evidence of dark matter in the Bullet Cluster galaxy collision.

The Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-558) is a pair of colliding galaxy clusters whose X-ray emitting gas has been displaced from the dominant gravitational mass traced by gravitational lensing — providing some of the most compelling evidence for the existence of dark matter. The dark matter haloes of the two clusters passed through each other nearly unimpeded, while the gas clouds slowed down due to electromagnetic interactions.

Circumstellar habitable zones shift outward as a star ages and brightens: the Sun was about 30% less luminous early in its history, yet Earth had liquid water — the 'faint young Sun paradox' remains an active research topic. On the other end, the Sun will brighten enough to evaporate Earth's oceans in about 1 to 1.5 billion years.

The Milky Way galaxy is estimated to contain roughly 400 million stellar-mass black holes — remnants of massive stars — but the vast majority are isolated and dark. Only those in binary systems actively accreting from a companion star or recently merged in gravitational wave events are detectable with current technology.

The Dragonfly 44 galaxy in the Coma Cluster, discovered in 2016, is a large 'ultra-diffuse galaxy' (UDG) that appears to be made of almost 99.99% dark matter. Its very low surface brightness and few visible stars yet high total mass — inferred from stellar velocity dispersions — initially puzzled astronomers, though follow-up studies have refined the dark matter fraction estimate.

Neutrinos produced in the Sun's core escape almost instantaneously, passing through the Sun's body in about two seconds, while the photons they accompany take between 10,000 and 170,000 years to random-walk from the core to the surface through repeated absorption and re-emission. Detecting solar neutrinos thus provides a direct window into the Sun's nuclear reactions happening right now.

The Perseverance rover, which landed in Jezero Crater on Mars in February 2021, is collecting rock cores for eventual return to Earth — the first Mars Sample Return mission in history if the retrieval campaign succeeds.
