It also carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which became the first powered aircraft to fly on another planet.

The photon sphere around a black hole is the radius at which gravity is strong enough that photons travel in circular orbits, located at 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius (3/2 r_s) for a non-rotating black hole. Light in the photon sphere is unstable — the slightest perturbation causes it to either fall into the black hole or escape to infinity, making it a key feature of the black hole shadow images.

The Great Wall (CfA2 Great Wall) discovered in 1989 is a sheet-like structure of galaxies roughly 500 million light-years long and 300 million light-years wide — one of the largest known structures in the universe at the time of its discovery. The subsequently discovered Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall spans an estimated 10 billion light-years and is currently the largest structure ever identified.

The cosmic recombination epoch occurred about 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the universe cooled enough for electrons and protons to combine into neutral hydrogen atoms. This made the universe transparent to photons for the first time, releasing the radiation we observe today as the cosmic microwave background.

GJ 1132b, a rocky exoplanet orbiting a nearby red dwarf 41 light-years away, was initially announced in 2015 as the most Earth-like exoplanet found around a nearby star at the time. Hubble observations later suggested it may have developed a secondary atmosphere — possibly volcanic in origin — after its original atmosphere was stripped by intense stellar radiation.

The Stephan's Quintet, a compact group of galaxies first observed in 1877 by Édouard Stephan, contains four galaxies that are genuinely interacting and one foreground galaxy seen in chance alignment. JWST's first released science image of this group revealed in exquisite detail the shock waves and star formation triggered by one galaxy plunging through the cluster at 800 kilometres per second.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic explosions in the universe, releasing more energy in seconds than the Sun will emit in its entire lifetime. They come in two classes: long GRBs (>2 seconds) associated with the collapse of massive stars into black holes, and short GRBs (<2 seconds) now confirmed to arise from neutron star mergers.

The Milky Way bar is thought to drive radial migration of stars from their birth orbits over billions of years, mixing the galactic disc and making it harder to reconstruct stellar birth environments from present-day positions. Chemical tagging — using the detailed elemental abundances of stars as chemical fingerprints — may allow astronomers to group stars back into their birth clusters despite this mixing.

The Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), a joint ESA/NASA mission launched in 1995, has become the most prolific comet discoverer in history — with nearly 4,000 comets found in its data, mostly by citizen scientists examining SOHO's coronagraph images online. It continuously monitors the Sun from the L1 Lagrange point and provides 24/7 space weather data.

Galaxy mergers trigger intense bursts of star formation by compressing gas clouds, producing starburst galaxies with star-formation rates hundreds to thousands of times higher than the Milky Way's quiescent rate. The resulting population of young massive stars ionises surrounding gas, drives powerful outflows, and enriches the galaxy's interstellar medium with metals on very short timescales.

The epoch of dark energy domination began about 4 to 5 billion years ago when the universe's expansion, previously decelerating under gravity, began accelerating due to the repulsive effect of dark energy. Prior to this, gravitational attraction dominated and galaxy clusters could grow; afterwards, structure formation on the largest scales was largely suppressed.

R136a1 in the Tarantula Nebula of the Large Magellanic Cloud is among the most massive stars ever observed, with an estimated mass of around 200 to 300 solar masses. Such extreme stars are so luminous that their radiation pressure pushes material off their surfaces at enormous rates, meaning they lose a significant fraction of their mass in stellar winds over their brief million-year lifetimes.

Cosmic strings are hypothetical one-dimensional topological defects in spacetime that may have formed during phase transitions in the very early universe, stretching across cosmological distances with extraordinary mass per unit length. Despite not being confirmed observationally, they remain a prediction of many grand unified theories and would be detectable through their gravitational wave signature.

Gamma-ray bursts were first accidentally discovered in the late 1960s by Vela military satellites designed to detect nuclear weapons tests in space. The discovery was classified for several years, and the first published report appeared in 1973; they remained one of astronomy's greatest mysteries until BeppoSAX detected the first X-ray afterglow in 1997, allowing optical and radio follow-up that pinpointed them in distant galaxies.

The Lyrid meteor shower, one of the oldest known meteor showers with records dating back to 687 BCE in China, peaks each year around April 22. It originates from debris left by Comet C/1861 G1 (Thatcher) and typically produces 10-20 meteors per hour at peak, though it occasionally surges to over 100 per hour during rare outbursts.

The theoretical maximum mass of a neutron star — the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit — is analogous to the Chandrasekhar limit for white dwarfs, but depends on poorly constrained nuclear matter physics at extreme densities. Current observations suggest the TOV limit is between about 2 and 3 solar masses, with the neutron star PSR J0952−0607 measured at about 2.35 solar masses being near the upper end of known neutron star masses.

The helium flash is a brief, explosive onset of helium fusion in the degenerate core of a low-mass red giant star when the core temperature reaches about 100 million Kelvin. Despite releasing enormous energy in seconds to minutes, the flash is invisible from outside the star because it is absorbed by the stellar envelope; the star readjusts its structure in less than a million years.

Cassini's discovery of active water-ice geysers on Enceladus in 2005 was one of the most stunning findings in planetary science in decades. The eruptions emerge through the famous 'tiger stripe' fractures at Enceladus's south pole, driven by heat from tidal flexing, and the material feeds Saturn's vast E ring.

The cosmic infrared background (CIB) is the integrated light from all galaxies in the history of the universe at infrared wavelengths, analogous to the cosmic optical background but detecting the emission reprocessed by dust. Measurements of the CIB place constraints on the total amount of star formation and black hole growth that has occurred across cosmic time.

Transit timing variations (TTVs) — deviations of exoplanet transit times from a perfectly periodic schedule — reveal the gravitational influence of additional unseen planets in the same system. This technique has been particularly powerful for detecting non-transiting planets and measuring the masses of transiting planets without requiring radial velocity measurements.

The coronagraph, invented by French astronomer Bernard Lyot in 1931, artificially blocks the Sun's bright disc to reveal the faint solar corona without needing a total solar eclipse. Modern space-based coronagraphs on SOHO and STEREO monitor the Sun continuously for coronal mass ejections that can trigger geomagnetic storms at Earth.

The galaxy cluster Abell 2029 contains a central giant elliptical galaxy — IC 1101 — that is one of the largest known galaxies in the universe, spanning about 6 million light-years in diameter. By comparison, the Milky Way is only about 100,000 light-years across; IC 1101 is thought to have grown so large by cannibalising dozens of smaller galaxies over billions of years.

The Tully-Fisher relation is an empirical correlation between a spiral galaxy's luminosity and its maximum rotation velocity (as measured by the 21-cm hydrogen line width). It is used as a distance indicator for spiral galaxies and has revealed that galaxy luminosities are tightly coupled to the depth of their dark matter gravitational potential wells.

The Hayashi track is a nearly vertical evolutionary path on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram along which a protostar descends while it contracts and heats up before reaching the main sequence. Fully convective protostars follow the Hayashi track, and its location sets the coolest possible temperature for a star in hydrostatic equilibrium.

The Spörer Minimum (1460–1550), Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), and Dalton Minimum (1790–1830) were prolonged periods of reduced sunspot activity associated with cooler temperatures in Europe, contributing to what climatologists call the Little Ice Age. The mechanisms linking solar activity to regional climate remain an active area of research.

Stellar winds from red giant stars are the primary mechanism by which carbon, oxygen, and other elements enriched by nuclear fusion are recycled back into the interstellar medium during the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase. A single AGB star can lose the equivalent of an Earth mass of enriched material every year over its final tens of thousands of years.

The Oort spike — a concentration of comets with orbital periods of millions of years incoming from the Oort Cloud for the first time — was identified by Jan Oort in 1950 and provided key evidence for the existence of a distant cometary reservoir. Oort noted that near-parabolic comets arrive from all directions in space, indicating a spherical rather than disc-shaped source.

The Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope (Roman Space Telescope, formerly WFIRST), planned for launch in the mid-2020s, will survey the sky in the near-infrared with a field of view 100 times larger than Hubble's. Its primary science goals include measuring the dark energy equation of state through a supernova survey and weak gravitational lensing of hundreds of millions of galaxies.

The Drake Equation's most uncertain term is the probability that intelligent life develops from simple life — a value we have exactly one data point for (Earth). Depending on pessimistic or optimistic interpretations of this factor, solutions to the Drake Equation range from much less than one technological civilisation in the galaxy today to millions.

Gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers carry away orbital energy and angular momentum as ripples in spacetime, causing the orbit to decay — a process called inspiral. In the milliseconds before merger, the objects are moving at a significant fraction of the speed of light and the gravitational wave frequency sweeps upward in a 'chirp' signal that LIGO's matched-filter algorithms are designed to detect.

Phosphorus — an essential element for DNA, RNA, and ATP — is one of the least abundant biologically relevant elements in the universe. Recent radio telescope observations of star-forming regions and the Cassini mission's analysis of Enceladus's ocean plumes have found dissolved phosphate, reinforcing that the basic chemistry of life may be widespread.

The galactic halo is a diffuse, roughly spherical component surrounding the Milky Way's visible disk that extends to distances of hundreds of kiloparsecs. It contains old metal-poor stars, globular clusters, and a large fraction of dark matter; the stellar halo's substructure — streams and shells from ancient mergers — is being mapped in exquisite detail by the Gaia satellite.

The planetary protection protocols maintained by NASA and ESA govern the sterilisation of spacecraft to prevent contaminating other worlds with Earth microbes (forward contamination) and prevent returning potentially dangerous extraterrestrial material to Earth (backward contamination). These protocols follow COSPAR guidelines and are most stringent for missions to environments considered potentially habitable, such as Mars, Europa, and Enceladus.

Infrared excess emission from a star — more infrared radiation than the stellar photosphere alone would produce — signals the presence of warm circumstellar dust in a debris disk. Vega, Fomalhaut, Epsilon Eridani, and Beta Pictoris were among the first stars discovered to have such disks by IRAS in 1983, suggesting they host ongoing collisions among planetesimals analogous to our own Kuiper Belt.

The Milky Way is currently being outrun in the local universe by the Great Attractor — a large overdensity of mass centred around the Norma Cluster about 250 million light-years away — which is pulling the Local Group at about 600 km/s. Mapping the Great Attractor was hampered for decades by the 'Zone of Avoidance' where dust and stars in the galactic plane block optical observations.

The solar minimum — the period of least sunspot activity between successive solar cycles — is when the Sun's magnetic field is most ordered and solar wind is slowest, which actually allows more galactic cosmic rays to penetrate the inner solar system. During solar maximum, the more turbulent magnetic field deflects these cosmic rays more effectively.

The Henize 2-10 galaxy is a nearby dwarf starburst galaxy that may contain a supermassive black hole actively participating in stimulating star formation rather than quenching it — the opposite of the typical 'AGN feedback' paradigm. Observations suggested a jet or outflow from the black hole is compressing gas in its path and triggering new star formation, providing a potential glimpse of how black holes and galaxies co-evolved in the early universe.

The Voyager 2 spacecraft remains the only human-made object to have flown past Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989), sending back the only close-up imagery and measurements we have of these distant ice giants. Its 1989 Neptune flyby revealed six previously unknown moons, a system of dark rings, and the Great Dark Spot — a storm analogous to Jupiter's Great Red Spot that has since dissipated.

The Coma Cluster (Abell 1656) was one of the first systems where Fritz Zwicky, in 1933, inferred the existence of what he called 'dark matter' — noting that the galaxies within the cluster were moving far too fast to be held together by the visible mass alone. This was the first strong evidence for hidden mass in the universe, predating the well-known galaxy rotation curve arguments by decades.

The Schwarzschild radius of an object is the critical radius at which, if all its mass were compressed within that sphere, its escape velocity equals the speed of light. For the Sun, this radius is about 3 kilometres; for Earth, it would be roughly 9 millimetres — illustrating that stellar-mass and planetary objects are far from their own Schwarzschild radii under normal conditions.

The WISE (Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer) telescope, launched in 2009, surveyed the entire sky in four infrared bands and discovered over 100,000 new asteroids and 33,000 near-Earth objects. Its all-sky maps also revealed hundreds of previously unknown brown dwarfs, including the discovery of a new spectral class called Y dwarfs — the coldest known brown dwarfs with temperatures below 500 K.

The magnetopause is the boundary between Earth's magnetosphere and the solar wind; its location on the dayside is roughly 10 Earth radii from the centre during quiet solar conditions. During strong geomagnetic storms, the increased solar wind pressure can compress the magnetopause to within 3 to 4 Earth radii, allowing energetic particles to penetrate closer to Earth.

The Pleiades (M45), sometimes called the Seven Sisters, is a young open cluster of hot blue stars about 444 light-years away and roughly 100 million years old. Ancient cultures worldwide — including Aboriginal Australians, the Maori, and the Greeks — independently identified and named this distinctive star cluster, often associating it with planting seasons or rainfall.

Jupiter's magnetosphere is the largest structure in the solar system, extending roughly 7 million km toward the Sun and over 700 million km in the anti-solar direction as a magnetotail. Its intense radiation belts trap electrons and protons accelerated to near-relativistic speeds, making them lethal to unshielded electronics — a significant challenge for the Juno and Europa Clipper missions.

Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe and in stars, but it is observed in space in several forms: neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), traced by its 21-cm radio emission; molecular hydrogen (H2), the main constituent of cold dense clouds; and ionised hydrogen (HII), glowing as emission nebulae around hot stars. Each phase dominates in different temperature and density regimes of the interstellar medium.

Milky Way's bar and spiral arm structure can be traced by mapping young massive stars, HII regions, and molecular gas clouds, which preferentially form in spiral arms. The Sun sits between the Sagittarius and Perseus Arms in the minor Orion Spur, putting it in a relatively calm inter-arm region — possibly a factor in Earth's relatively stable geological and biological history.

The helioseismology technique uses oscillations of the solar surface — sound waves ringing through the Sun's interior — to map layers deep within the Sun that are otherwise inaccessible. It revealed the sharp boundary between the radiative zone and convection zone (the tachocline) and has been used to test stellar interior models with unprecedented precision.

The zodiacal cloud — also called the interplanetary dust cloud — extends from the Sun out to the asteroid belt and beyond, maintained by a steady supply of dust from cometary debris and asteroid collisions. Earth sweeps through denser dust trails left by short-period comets each year, producing the annual meteor showers that light up the night sky.

The dwarf planet Haumea, discovered in 2004, is one of the fastest rotating large objects in the solar system — completing a rotation every 3.9 hours — and this rapid spin has flattened it into an oblate spheroid roughly twice as long as it is wide. Haumea also has a faint ring system discovered in 2017 and two small moons, Hi'iaka and Namaka.

The Parker instability is a magnetohydrodynamic instability in which the magnetic field threading a galaxy's gas disc becomes top-heavy, causing gas to slide downward and magnetic fields to buckle upward into the halo. This process helps explain how large-scale magnetic field loops are maintained in spiral galaxies and contributes to the formation of giant molecular cloud complexes.

The Eta Carinae binary system, roughly 7,500 light-years away, is one of the most massive and luminous stellar systems known, with a combined luminosity about 5 million times the Sun. In 1843 it briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky during the 'Great Eruption,' ejecting about 10–40 solar masses of material that now form the Homunculus Nebula surrounding it.

The Sombrero Galaxy (M104) is a remarkable edge-on spiral galaxy with an unusually prominent dust lane and a large central bulge — one of the most distinctive objects in Messier's catalogue. Its central region hosts one of the most massive black holes in any nearby galaxy, estimated at about 1 billion solar masses.

The cosmic neutrino background is estimated to contribute about 0.1–0.7% of the total energy density of the universe, depending on neutrino masses. Although neutrinos travel at nearly the speed of light and pass through matter almost unhindered, their collective mass — still uncertain but constrained to below about 0.12 eV per flavour by cosmological observations — has measurable effects on the growth of large-scale structure.

The Martian moon Phobos has a very low average density of about 1.876 g/cm³ — less than most rock types — suggesting it may be a rubble pile held together by a thin regolith shell rather than a solid body. Its large crater Stickney, 9 km across (roughly half the moon's own diameter), is testament to a near-catastrophic ancient impact.

The epoch of reionisation ended around redshift z ~ 6 (about 900 million years after the Big Bang), as inferred from the Gunn-Peterson troughs — complete absorption of quasar spectra at wavelengths shorter than Lyman-alpha — seen in distant quasars. These troughs indicate dense patches of neutral hydrogen gas that had not yet been ionised by the first stars and galaxies.

The Arrokoth contact binary — the first pristine Kuiper Belt Object ever closely imaged, visited by New Horizons in January 2019 — appears uniformly reddish due to tholins (complex organic compounds) formed by radiation processing of methanol ice. Its gentle bilobed shape indicates that the two lobes formed separately from the same rotating cloud and came together in a slow merger, supporting the pebble accretion model of planet formation.

The Trapezium Cluster in the heart of the Orion Nebula is one of the youngest and closest known regions of ongoing massive star formation, only about 1,500 light-years away. Its four central massive O-type stars — visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch — have only recently dispersed the gas cloud from which they formed, illuminating the surrounding nebulosity.

The concept of dark energy was introduced in 1998 following the discovery by two independent teams (led by Saul Perlmutter and by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess) that Type Ia supernovae at high redshift were dimmer than expected, indicating the universe's expansion is accelerating rather than decelerating. This discovery earned Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Proxima Centauri — the Sun's closest stellar neighbour at 4.24 light-years — is a red dwarf that hosts at least one confirmed rocky planet, Proxima b, in its habitable zone. Despite being in the habitable zone, Proxima b may face challenges for habitability due to intense flares from its host star that could strip its atmosphere and bombard its surface with ionising radiation.

The Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus) in the Large Magellanic Cloud is the most active star-forming region in the Local Group, glowing across tens of thousands of light-years. If it were as close to Earth as the Orion Nebula, it would be so bright that it cast visible shadows at night.

Astronomical masers — naturally occurring microwave lasers in space — are produced when population inversions in molecules like water (H2O), hydroxyl (OH), methanol (CH3OH), and silicon monoxide (SiO) in circumstellar envelopes, star-forming regions, or active galaxies emit coherent, highly beamed microwave radiation. Water masers in the galaxy NGC 4258 have been used to measure its distance and the Hubble constant independently.

Stellar ages can be estimated through gyrochronology — the observation that stars spin down predictably as they age due to magnetic braking by their stellar winds. Younger stars rotate faster; measuring a star's rotation period (via starspot modulation of its light curve) and its mass therefore gives an age estimate accurate to about 10–15% for main-sequence stars up to a few billion years old.

The 21-centimetre hydrogen line — emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom flips its spin relative to the nucleus — has been essential for mapping neutral hydrogen throughout the Milky Way, revealing the galaxy's spiral structure. Its frequency (1,420 MHz) is also one of the frequencies searched by SETI as a potentially universal 'watering hole' frequency where an advanced civilisation might broadcast.

Titan's atmospheric haze — the orange smog giving it its distinctive color — consists of aerosol particles called tholins, complex organic molecules formed when ultraviolet light and Saturn's magnetospheric electrons react with nitrogen and methane. Similar chemistry may have operated on early Earth before photosynthesis oxygenated the atmosphere.

The exoplanet system Kepler-90, discovered by the Kepler mission, has eight confirmed planets — the same number as our solar system — making it the first known star other than the Sun confirmed to host that many planets. The eighth planet, Kepler-90i, was identified in 2017 using machine learning trained on the Kepler data set.

The ecliptic — the apparent path of the Sun against the background stars over the course of a year — is the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most solar system planets orbit close to the ecliptic because they formed from the same rotating protoplanetary disk, while comets and Oort Cloud objects can have highly inclined orbits from any direction.

The ice line (or frost line) in a protoplanetary disk is the distance from the central star beyond which temperatures are low enough for volatile compounds like water, ammonia, and methane to condense into solid ice grains. Jupiter formed just beyond the water ice line in our solar system, giving it access to abundant solid material that allowed rapid growth before the disk dissipated.

The Fermi bubbles are two enormous lobes of gamma-ray and X-ray emitting plasma extending about 25,000 light-years above and below the Milky Way's galactic plane, discovered by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope in 2010. They were probably produced by powerful past activity from Sgr A* or intense star formation near the galactic centre about 2 to 8 million years ago.

The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect has been used by the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) to discover hundreds of previously unknown galaxy clusters at high redshifts. These surveys provide cosmological constraints on dark energy and the sum of neutrino masses by counting how cluster abundance evolves over cosmic time.

Water ice has been confirmed in permanently shadowed craters near the lunar poles, where temperatures never rise above about −170°C. These deposits — estimated to contain hundreds of millions to billions of metric tons of water ice — are a key resource for potential future lunar bases, providing drinking water, oxygen, and rocket propellant.

The Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/4039) are a pair of colliding spiral galaxies about 45 million light-years away whose long tidal tails — resembling insect antennae — were formed by gravitational tidal forces during their interaction. They host hundreds of brilliant young star clusters formed in the collision, and the merger will likely be complete in about 400 million years.

The cosmic coincidence problem notes that the energy densities of matter and dark energy are of the same order of magnitude today (~30% and ~70%), despite the fact that dark energy density remains roughly constant while matter density decreases as the universe expands. The probability that we happen to live at the cosmic epoch when these two completely different energy components are comparable seems remarkably small.

The Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism — energy released by gravitational contraction — powered the Sun and other stars before nuclear fusion was understood. Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz calculated that contraction could power the Sun for only 15–20 million years, far less than the geological record demanded; the mystery was not resolved until Hans Bethe worked out the nuclear fusion pp chain in 1939.

Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system — larger even than the planet Mercury — and the only moon known to have its own internally generated magnetic field, which creates a small magnetosphere embedded within Jupiter's much larger magnetosphere. The ESA JUICE mission launched in 2023 aims to orbit Ganymede starting around 2034.

The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula (M16), one of the most iconic Hubble images captured in 1995 and revisited by JWST in 2022, are towering columns of cold gas and dust where new stars are actively forming. The infrared JWST image revealed hundreds of previously hidden newly forming stars embedded in the dust columns, confirming ongoing star birth.

Stellar chromospheres — the thin layer just above a star's photosphere — can be detected by the distinctive emission cores in the centres of the calcium H and K absorption lines in stellar spectra. The Mount Wilson Observatory Ca HK monitoring programme followed hundreds of stars over decades, revealing that many sun-like stars undergo activity cycles analogous to our 11-year solar cycle.

The Bode-Titius (or Titius-Bode) law is an empirical rule suggesting that planetary orbital distances follow a simple exponential sequence, fitting the known planets from Mercury to Uranus (and predicting a 'missing' planet between Mars and Jupiter where the asteroid belt is). While it accurately predicted Uranus's position and the asteroid belt, it fails for Neptune and is no longer considered a physically fundamental relationship.

The Euclid space telescope, launched by ESA in July 2023, is designed to map the geometry and dark matter distribution of the large-scale universe by precisely measuring the shapes of billions of galaxies using weak gravitational lensing and baryon acoustic oscillations. Its six-year survey will cover one third of the sky and probe the history of dark energy from redshift 2 to the present day.

The concept of the observable universe horizon exists because light has had a finite time (13.8 billion years) to travel since the Big Bang, but the expansion of space has stretched those photons' origin points to about 46 billion light-years away today. Objects beyond this particle horizon are not merely difficult to see — their light literally has not had time to reach us.

The South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) is a region above the South Atlantic Ocean where Earth's inner Van Allen radiation belt dips closest to the surface, exposing orbiting spacecraft and the International Space Station to elevated radiation. Astronauts on the ISS sometimes see phosphene flashes when cosmic rays pass through their eyes as they traverse the SAA.

The Great Observatories programme of NASA comprised four space telescopes designed to survey the sky across different wavelengths: the Hubble Space Telescope (optical/UV/IR), the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (gamma rays), the Chandra X-ray Observatory (X-rays), and the Spitzer Space Telescope (infrared). Together they revolutionised multi-wavelength astronomy from the 1990s through the 2020s.

The Stephan's Quintet galaxy group contains the most distant member of a compact group and four galaxies undergoing one of the largest known galaxy collisions, producing a giant intergalactic shock wave more than 100,000 light-years wide. Observations at multiple wavelengths — from X-ray (Chandra) to infrared (JWST) — have revealed complex turbulent gas heating and star formation in the shock.

Planetary migration — the large-scale movement of planets from their formation locations due to gravitational interactions with the gas disk or with other planets — is thought to have dramatically restructured our own solar system. The Nice model proposes that Jupiter and Saturn migrated slightly, triggering a dynamical instability that scattered Uranus and Neptune outward and caused the Late Heavy Bombardment on the inner planets around 4 billion years ago.

Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are large expulsions of plasma and magnetic field from the solar corona that can contain up to 10^13 kg of material travelling at speeds of 250–3000 km/s. When a CME is directed toward Earth, it can cause severe geomagnetic storms, disrupt power grids, damage satellites, and produce spectacular auroras visible at unusually low latitudes.

The HR 8799 exoplanetary system, directly imaged in 2008, has four giant planets discovered through direct imaging — one of only a handful of multi-planet systems imaged this way. A subsequent study combined 10 years of imaging data into a movie showing the planets actually moving in their orbits, providing a rare direct visual demonstration of planetary orbital motion around another star.

The Messier Catalogue, compiled by French astronomer Charles Messier in the 18th century, lists 110 deep-sky objects — nebulae, star clusters, and galaxies — that he documented to avoid confusing them with comets he was searching for. Many of the most iconic objects in the night sky, from the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) to the Orion Nebula (M42), bear Messier numbers.

The cosmic shear signal — the coherent distortion of galaxy shapes by gravitational lensing due to large-scale structure along the line of sight — is one of the most powerful probes of the dark matter distribution and dark energy. The Dark Energy Survey (DES), Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC), and KiDS surveys have measured cosmic shear across hundreds of square degrees, providing constraints on cosmological parameters competitive with CMB measurements.

Spectral lines of molecules in cold interstellar clouds can reveal a cloud's line-of-sight velocity through the Doppler shift, and its rotation temperature through the ratio of intensities of different rotational transitions. Radio astronomers have identified over 200 distinct molecular species in the interstellar medium, including complex organic molecules like glycolaldehyde, ethyl formate, and even the amino acid glycine (tentatively).

The cosmic optical background (COB) is the integrated visible-light emission from all galaxies across cosmic history. Its total brightness implies that, on average, the universe has produced far more stars than observations of individual galaxies had previously suggested — indicating that many photons come from stars in the faint outskirts of galaxies or in low-surface-brightness galaxies too diffuse to be easily counted.

The Penrose process is a mechanism by which energy can be extracted from a rotating (Kerr) black hole by splitting a particle inside the ergosphere — a region outside the event horizon where no stationary observers can exist — such that one piece falls in with negative energy, allowing the other to escape with more energy than the original particle had. This process may power the relativistic jets seen in some active galactic nuclei.

The Geminid meteor shower, which peaks around December 13–14 each year, produces meteors that are typically slower and more colourful than those from most other showers because they enter Earth's atmosphere at a somewhat lower relative velocity (~35 km/s vs ~66 km/s for Leonids). The higher average density of Phaethon's debris compared to typical cometary dust also makes Geminid meteors more durable.

Io's intense volcanic activity was predicted by Stanton Peale, Patrick Cassen, and Ray Reynolds in a landmark paper published the week before Voyager 1's 1979 flyby confirmed active volcanism. Their calculation showed tidal heating from Jupiter would generate enormous internal heat — an extraordinary predictive triumph of planetary science.

Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAOs) are a fixed physical scale imprinted in the distribution of galaxies, corresponding to the distance sound waves could travel in the early universe before recombination — about 150 megaparsecs (490 million light-years) in today's units. BAOs serve as a 'standard ruler' for measuring cosmic distances across billions of light-years and constraining the history of dark energy.

Gravitational redshift — the stretching of photon wavelengths as they climb out of a gravitational potential well — was first predicted by Einstein in 1907 and confirmed in the solar spectrum in the 1920s. It was measured with extraordinary precision in 1959 in a ground-based experiment by Pound and Rebka at Harvard, validating general relativity to 10% accuracy using gamma rays over a 22-metre height difference.

The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the world's premier locations for astronomy due to its extreme altitude, dryness (some areas receive no measurable rainfall for years), and stable atmospheric conditions. It hosts ALMA, Paranal Observatory (VLT), La Silla, and the sites for the ELT and Rubin Observatory, making it arguably the densest concentration of world-class telescopes on Earth.

Neptune's largest moon Triton orbits in a retrograde direction — opposite to Neptune's rotation — and is the only large moon in the solar system to do so. This is strong evidence that Triton was not formed alongside Neptune but was captured from the Kuiper Belt; its retrograde orbit is slowly decaying, and in about 3.6 billion years it will break apart to form a ring system.

The Active Cavity Radiometer Irradiance Monitor (ACRIM) and subsequent instruments have measured total solar irradiance from space since 1980, finding that it varies by about 0.1% over the 11-year solar cycle. This small variation is insufficient to explain recent climate change on Earth but may modulate regional climate patterns.

The Magellanic Stream is a ribbon of gas spanning about 300 degrees of sky stretching from the Magellanic Clouds toward and beyond the South Galactic Pole, tidally and ram-pressure stripped from the Magellanic Clouds over hundreds of millions of years. It is thought to represent a significant future gas supply for the Milky Way's star formation.

The Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale Crater on Mars in August 2012, confirmed that the crater once held a long-lived lake of liquid water with neutral pH, low salinity, and chemical energy sources — conditions suitable for chemolithotrophic microbes if they had ever existed there. It detected organic molecules including thiophenes, benzene, and toluene preserved in ancient mudstones.

Photometric redshift estimation uses the colours of a galaxy measured in several broad photometric bands to estimate its redshift without spectroscopy. This technique allows very large galaxy surveys (like those from DES, HSC, and eventually Rubin) to assign approximate distances to hundreds of millions of objects far faster than spectroscopic surveys could.

The Milky Way's thick disk contains older, more metal-poor stars than the thin disk and has a higher scale height — the stars don't settle as flat. Gaia astrometry combined with spectroscopy has revealed that the thick disk is largely the remnant of a major merger event (the Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage merger) that occurred about 10 billion years ago, depositing stars and building up the inner galaxy.

The Kepler second law states that a line connecting a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times — meaning planets move faster near perihelion (closest approach to the Sun) and slower near aphelion (farthest point). This law, deduced empirically by Kepler in 1609, is a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

Stellar occultations by Pluto's thin nitrogen atmosphere have been monitored since 1988 and revealed that Pluto's surface pressure doubled between 1988 and 2016 despite moving further from the Sun — driven by nitrogen sublimating from Tombaugh Regio's vast nitrogen ice plains exposed to sunlight. This was one of the key motivations for New Horizons' flyby in 2015.

The Uhuru satellite (SAS-1), launched in 1970, was the first space observatory dedicated entirely to X-ray astronomy and conducted the first comprehensive survey of X-ray sources in the sky. Its discovery of the first strong evidence for a stellar-mass black hole in Cygnus X-1 (through its binary orbit with a companion star) was a landmark in astrophysics.

Stellar winds from massive O and B stars can generate superbubbles — enormous cavities blown into the interstellar medium, hundreds of light-years across, bounded by a shell of swept-up gas and dust. When a massive star explodes as a supernova inside such a bubble, the shock wave travels faster and farther than it would in undisturbed ISM, distributing heavy elements widely through the galaxy.

Gravitational potential energy drives stellar evolution: as a main-sequence star exhausts its hydrogen core fuel, it contracts, heating the core and expanding the envelope into a red giant phase. This seemingly paradoxical behaviour — contracting the core while expanding the outer layers — is known as the mirror principle in stellar physics.

The HII region NGC 604 in the Triangulum Galaxy (M33) is the largest emission nebula in the Local Group — about 1,500 light-years across and 6,300 light-years away from Earth — hosting over 200 very hot O-type stars whose ultraviolet radiation ionises the surrounding gas. It is roughly 40 times the diameter of the Orion Nebula.

Mascons (mass concentrations) are regions of anomalously high gravitational fields beneath the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and other solid bodies, caused by dense subsurface basaltic lava flows that flooded ancient impact basins. They were discovered in 1968 using precise Doppler tracking of the Lunar Orbiter spacecraft and must be accounted for in mission planning for lunar and Martian orbiters.

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is visible to the naked eye as a faint fuzzy patch of light in the constellation Andromeda, making it the most distant object visible without optical aid at about 2.537 million light-years. The light reaching your eyes from Andromeda tonight left the galaxy when Homo erectus was roaming the Earth.

Gravitational waves can be produced by any accelerating mass distribution but only emit detectable signals when the masses involved are enormous and moving at relativistic speeds. The characteristic 'chirp' frequency of a black hole binary merger sweeps from a few hertz up to a few hundred hertz — coinciding with the sensitive band of LIGO — over the final seconds before the black holes coalesce.

The Milky Way's disk is warped — it is not flat but curves upward on one side and downward on the other, an asymmetry extending to the galaxy's outer regions. Recent Gaia data and studies of Cepheid variable stars confirmed this warp and suggested it may have been caused by the gravitational pull of the Magellanic Clouds or by a past interaction with a satellite galaxy.

The Lyman break galaxy technique identifies star-forming galaxies at high redshift (z ~ 3) by their characteristic sharp dropout in blue light: hydrogen in the galaxy's interstellar medium and circumgalactic medium absorbs essentially all photons shortward of the Lyman limit (912 Å). This technique, pioneered by Charles Steidel in the early 1990s, allowed the first systematic surveys of the galaxy population in the young universe.

Saturn's polar hexagon — a remarkable hexagonal jet stream with sides about 14,000 km long at Saturn's north pole — was first observed by Voyager spacecraft in 1981 and has persisted unchanged for decades as of Cassini observations. Laboratory fluid dynamics experiments show that similar hexagonal patterns form naturally in rotating flows under certain conditions.

The first extrasolar planet discovered around a main-sequence Sun-like star was 51 Pegasi b in 1995, a hot Jupiter orbiting its star every 4.23 days at only about 1/20th the Earth-Sun distance. Its discovery by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz using the radial velocity technique upended theories of planet formation and opened the modern era of exoplanet science.

The Compton wavelength of a particle is a quantum mechanical length scale inversely proportional to its mass, below which quantum field theory effects become important. For black holes, comparing the Schwarzschild radius to the Compton wavelength gives the Planck mass — about 22 micrograms — the scale at which quantum gravitational effects become as important as classical general relativity.

The Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) installed on Hubble in 2009 has revolutionised ultraviolet spectroscopy of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) — the largely invisible gas in the cosmic web filaments that contains up to half of all ordinary baryonic matter in the low-redshift universe. COS observations of UV absorption features in background quasar spectra have directly detected and characterised this long-sought 'missing' baryons.

Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) — the study of the behaviour of electrically conducting fluids in magnetic fields — governs the dynamics of the Sun, solar wind, planetary magnetospheres, and much of the interstellar medium. The magnetic reconnection process, in which magnetic field lines in a plasma suddenly rearrange topology and release stored energy explosively, drives solar flares, geomagnetic substorms, and energetic particle acceleration.

The zodiac originally had 13 constellations before the Babylonians standardised the system to 12, dropping Ophiuchus. Today the Sun actually passes through Ophiuchus for 19 days between November 29 and December 17, but it remains the unofficial '13th sign' of the zodiac — a fact that periodically creates confusion when astronomers point it out.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) installed on the Mayall Telescope at Kitt Peak, Arizona, uses 5,000 robotic optical fibres to simultaneously take spectra of 5,000 galaxies and quasars. Its primary goal is to measure baryon acoustic oscillations across cosmic time using tens of millions of galaxy spectra, producing the largest 3D map of the universe ever created.

Cassini's 2017 'Grand Finale' dives between Saturn and its rings sent back unprecedented data about the planet's interior, magnetic field, and the mass and composition of the rings. The data confirmed the rings are geologically young — probably only 100 to 400 million years old — and revealed that Saturn's day is 10 hours, 33 minutes, and 38 seconds long.

Seyfert galaxies are a class of active galaxy with very bright, compact nuclei and broad emission lines indicating rapidly moving hot gas near a central supermassive black hole. Carl Seyfert identified them in 1943, making them the first recognised class of active galactic nuclei; they are subdivided into Type 1 (broad and narrow emission lines visible) and Type 2 (only narrow lines, with the broad-line region hidden by dust).

The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), currently under construction at sites in La Palma and Chile, will be the world's largest and most sensitive very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray observatory. It will use arrays of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes that detect the brief blue light flashes produced when VHE gamma rays interact with Earth's atmosphere.

The Io plasma torus is a donut-shaped belt of sulfur and oxygen ions orbiting Jupiter at Io's orbital radius, fed by material from Io's volcanic plumes that gets ionised by Jupiter's magnetospheric electrons. It glows in ultraviolet light and radiates about 1 trillion watts of power — intercepting and affecting the orbits of Jupiter's inner moons.

The LIGO scientific collaboration operates two L-shaped interferometers in the United States (in Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana) each with 4-km-long arms. The detectors measure strain — changes in arm length — as small as 1/10,000th the diameter of a proton caused by a passing gravitational wave, achieved through quantum optics and sophisticated vibration isolation systems.

The galactic thin disk is about 1,000 light-years thick and hosts most of the Milky Way's current star formation, while the thick disk extends about 3,400 light-years above and below the galactic midplane. The Sun orbits the galactic centre with a slight vertical oscillation, dipping above and below the midplane with a period of roughly 70 million years — sometimes proposed as a trigger for periodic extinction events on Earth.

The spectral energy distribution (SED) of a galaxy — its brightness measured at many different wavelengths — encodes information about its stellar populations, star formation history, dust content, and AGN activity. SED fitting uses models of stellar populations and dust emission to simultaneously constrain all these properties from broadband photometric data.

Cometary nuclei are often described as 'dirty snowballs' — a term coined by Fred Whipple in 1950 — composed of ice, frozen gases, and dust. ESA's Rosetta mission revealed that Comet 67P has an extremely dark surface (albedo ~6%), an irregular 'rubber duck' shape, and jets of gas and dust actively erupting from sunlit regions — painting a complex picture of cometary surfaces.

The total number of stars in the observable universe is estimated at around 200 to 400 sextillion (2–4 × 10^23), based on the number of galaxies (~2 trillion) multiplied by the average number of stars per galaxy (~100 billion). This number exceeds the estimated number of grains of sand on all Earth's beaches by a factor of roughly 10,000.

Barnard's Star, a red dwarf 5.96 light-years away and the fourth-nearest star to the Sun, has the largest proper motion of any known star — moving about 10.36 arcseconds per year across the sky. At its current velocity, it will reach its closest approach to the Sun of about 3.75 light-years in roughly 10,000 years.

The cosmic ray spectrum spans over 12 orders of magnitude in energy, from about 10^9 eV to beyond 10^20 eV, following a power law with two notable breaks called the 'knee' (~10^15.5 eV) and 'ankle' (~10^18.5 eV). The knee is thought to mark the maximum energy achievable by supernovae-driven acceleration in the Milky Way, while particles above the ankle are believed to be of extragalactic origin.

The stellar initial mass function (IMF) describes how stars of different masses form from a molecular cloud, first parameterised by Edwin Salpeter in 1955. Most stars form with relatively low masses (0.1–1 solar masses), but massive stars (>8 solar masses) — though rare — dominate the light output of young stellar populations and control the chemical enrichment of galaxies through supernovae.

The Poynting-Robertson effect causes small dust particles in the solar system to slowly spiral inward toward the Sun due to the radiation pressure force: as a particle orbits, it absorbs sunlight and re-emits it slightly forward — transferring momentum and causing a slight drag that removes orbital energy over thousands to millions of years. This effect keeps the zodiacal dust cloud from accumulating over geological time.

The Omega Centauri globular cluster, about 17,000 light-years from Earth, contains evidence for multiple stellar populations with different ages and chemical compositions — unusual for globular clusters, which are typically thought to be single-age, single-composition systems. It is now widely believed to be the stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy cannibalised by the Milky Way.

The Pioneer anomaly — an unexplained deceleration experienced by Pioneer 10 and 11 pointing toward the Sun at about 8.74 × 10^-10 m/s² — puzzled physicists for two decades and briefly inspired proposals for new physics. It was ultimately resolved in 2012 by a careful analysis of anisotropic thermal radiation recoil from the spacecraft's radioisotope thermoelectric generators.

The Sloan Great Wall, discovered in 2003 in SDSS data, spans approximately 1.37 billion light-years — at the time the largest known structure in the universe. It is a sheet-like concentration of galaxies at a redshift of about z = 0.07–0.08, and while superseded by discoveries of larger structures, it remains one of the most impressive examples of large-scale cosmic structure.

The accretion disc around a black hole is an extremely hot, flat structure of gas and dust spiralling inward as it loses angular momentum through viscosity driven by magnetorotational instability (MRI). The innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) — at 3 Schwarzschild radii for a non-rotating black hole, smaller for a spinning one — marks where infalling material plunges into the black hole.

The S2 star, orbiting Sgr A* on a 16-year elliptical orbit, reached pericentre (closest approach) in 2018 and the resulting gravitational redshift was detected spectroscopically — providing the first direct measurement of general relativistic effects in the strong-field regime near the galactic centre black hole. The star's orbit comes within about 120 AU of Sgr A*.

The Draco Dwarf Galaxy, discovered in 1954 by Albert Wilson, is one of the least luminous galaxies known, containing only about 260,000 solar luminosities of stars. Yet it has a very large total mass inferred from stellar velocities, giving it an extraordinary mass-to-light ratio suggesting it is almost entirely composed of dark matter — making such ultra-faint dwarfs among the purest dark matter laboratories.

The North Star (Polaris) is not exactly at the celestial north pole but currently about 0.7 degrees away, slowly approaching the pole until its closest approach of about 0.45 degrees in 2100 before moving away again. Polaris is itself a binary system — a Cepheid variable star with a fainter companion — making it a convenient multi-purpose tool for both navigation and stellar physics.

Phosphine (PH3) was detected in trace amounts in Jupiter's upper atmosphere in 2022 using JWST data, confirming earlier detections from Cassini and ground-based facilities. Jupiter's phosphine is thought to originate in its deep interior — where temperature and pressure are high enough to form it — and is dredged up by convection to altitudes where it would otherwise be rapidly destroyed by ultraviolet light.

The Hipparcos mission (1989–1993) was ESA's first dedicated astrometry satellite and measured the precise positions, parallaxes, and proper motions of over 100,000 stars, extending the cosmic distance ladder by ten times the reach of ground-based parallax measurements. The Gaia mission, Hipparcos's successor, has improved precision by a further factor of 100 while measuring over a billion stars.

The Zodiacal Catalogue stars — the fundamental reference frame for astrometry — are being replaced by the Gaia Celestial Reference Frame (Gaia-CRF) tied to distant quasars, making it inertial to unprecedented precision. This shift from a star-based to a quasar-based reference frame eliminates systematic errors from proper motions of reference stars.

Haumea's ring system, announced in 2017, was discovered through a stellar occultation campaign that showed symmetrical brightness dips before and after the dwarf planet blocked a star. At roughly 3,100 km from Haumea's centre, the ring sits at the 3:1 spin-orbit resonance, making it dynamically stable — a different mechanism than Saturn's rings.

Gravitational lensing by galaxy clusters produces spectacular 'arcs' and 'arclets' — stretched images of background galaxies bent into curved streaks by the cluster's gravitational field. By measuring the distortion pattern, astronomers can reconstruct the cluster's total mass distribution, including dark matter, far more directly than from visible light or X-ray observations alone.

Io's surface is continuously resurfaced by volcanic activity at a rate estimated at about 1.3 cm per year on average — fast enough that the moon's surface has no visible impact craters. This makes Io unique among solar system bodies: it is the only object whose surface is effectively 'erased' by volcanism faster than craters accumulate.

The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event was a major merger between the proto-Milky Way and a dwarf galaxy of about one-third the Milky Way's mass around 10 billion years ago. Evidence from Gaia astrometry shows a large population of halo stars with highly radial, elongated orbits — the 'Sausage' shape in velocity space — that are the kinematically distinct debris of the accreted galaxy.

Asteroid Bennu, the target of the OSIRIS-REx mission, was found to be a carbon-rich rubble pile in a very slow retrograde spin with unexpected boulder-covered terrain suggesting ongoing surface geological activity. In October 2023, OSIRIS-REx successfully returned samples from Bennu's surface to Earth, delivering the largest asteroid sample collection in history — over 120 grams of material.

The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect's spectral signature is unique: it decreases the CMB intensity at frequencies below 217 GHz and increases it above — the opposite of any emission from an astronomical object. This distinctive spectral change allows galaxy clusters to be identified against the CMB even at very high redshifts where their optical brightness would be negligible.

Milky Way's nuclear stellar disk — a compact structure of stars within the central few hundred light-years — is chemically and kinematically distinct from the surrounding bulge. The GALACSI/NFM adaptive optics system on the VLT has recently resolved individual stars in this crowded environment, revealing chemically enriched stellar populations and extreme stellar density.

The night side of Venus, viewed in infrared, glows with thermal emission from its lower atmosphere — a natural phenomenon used by the VIRTIS instrument on Venus Express to study Venus's lower atmospheric temperature structure through its otherwise opaque cloud deck. This technique revealed unexpected asymmetries in the lower atmosphere's circulation pattern.

The cosmic background neutrinos produced in the first second after the Big Bang have such low energies today (around 0.00017 eV) that detecting them directly has so far been impossible. PTOLEMY, a proposed experiment, aims to detect the cosmic neutrino background through neutrino capture on tritium — a reaction that would produce a tiny peak in the electron energy spectrum slightly above the normal tritium beta-decay endpoint.

The eclipsing binary star Algol (Beta Persei) was among the first variable stars recognised and gave rise to the concept of an eclipsing system. It was studied by John Goodricke in 1783, who correctly inferred that its regular dimming every 2.87 days was caused by a darker companion periodically passing in front of a brighter star — remarkable reasoning for an 18-year-old who was deaf.

Wolf-Rayet stars are an extreme class of massive evolved stars that have shed most of their hydrogen envelopes and are rapidly losing mass through powerful stellar winds at rates up to 10^-4 solar masses per year — losing a solar mass in just 10,000 years. Their spectra are dominated by broad emission lines of helium, carbon, oxygen, or nitrogen, depending on their evolutionary stage.

The cosmic star-formation history peaks at redshift z ~ 2 (about 10 billion years ago), an epoch sometimes called 'cosmic noon,' when the universe formed stars at a rate roughly ten times higher than today. Since then, star formation has gradually declined — partly because gas reservoirs are depleted and partly because AGN feedback from supermassive black holes quenches star formation in the most massive galaxies.

Stellar streams are the remnant tidal debris of disrupted globular clusters or dwarf galaxies, spread along the former orbit as a narrow band of stars. The Sagittarius Stream wraps at least twice around the Milky Way and has been used to measure the shape and mass of our galaxy's dark matter halo; dozens of additional streams have been identified by Gaia and SDSS.

Ceres, the only dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, was discovered in 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi — the first asteroid ever found — and was classified as a planet for several decades before being demoted when more belt objects were discovered. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited Ceres from 2015 to 2018 and discovered bright spots in Occator Crater, revealing brine-rich liquid reservoirs that once erupted to the surface.

The giant arc — a giant curved structure of galaxies spanning about 3.3 billion light-years discovered in SDSS data in 2021 — is one of the largest single structures known in the universe and may challenge the cosmological principle (the assumption that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales). Structures this large should be vanishingly rare according to standard cosmological models.

Nuclear pasta — theoretical exotic states of matter in the crust of neutron stars where protons and neutrons arrange into spaghetti-like, lasagne-like, or Swiss-cheese topologies due to competing nuclear and electromagnetic forces — is theorised to be the strongest material in the universe, with a shear modulus roughly 10 billion times that of steel. Its properties affect how neutron star crusts crack and emit gravitational waves.

The galactic rotation curve of the Milky Way — showing how the circular velocity of stars and gas varies with distance from the galactic centre — stays roughly flat at about 220 km/s out to the limits of measurement rather than decreasing as Keplerian physics would predict for a concentrated mass. This flatness is among the strongest pieces of evidence for a massive, extended dark matter halo surrounding our galaxy.

The Allen Telescope Array (ATA) in Hat Creek, California, consists of 42 small dish antennas working together as an interferometer — designed from the start as a dual-use facility for radio astronomy and SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) surveys. Its design allows simultaneous astronomical observation and targeted SETI surveys of thousands of nearby stars.

Makemake, one of the largest known Kuiper Belt Objects and a dwarf planet, has no confirmed moon unlike other similarly sized KBOs. Its surface is covered with frozen methane and ethane that give it a reddish colour, and it has no detectable atmosphere, unlike Pluto, because it orbits slightly further from the Sun and its methane does not sublimate as readily.

Atmospheric transparency windows — narrow wavelength ranges where Earth's atmosphere is relatively transparent to electromagnetic radiation — determine where ground-based telescopes can operate. Major windows exist in the visible, near-infrared, and radio bands; gamma-ray, X-ray, far-ultraviolet, far-infrared, and most microwave observations must be conducted from space.

The population of exoplanets with sizes between 1.5 and 2 Earth radii is notably rare compared to smaller and larger planets — a gap in the size distribution called the 'radius valley' or 'Fulton gap.' This is thought to result from photoevaporation: stellar X-ray and UV radiation strips the atmospheres of planets that are too small to retain them, leaving behind bare rocky super-Earths.

The Milky Way's central molecular zone (CMZ) — the innermost few hundred light-years of the galaxy — contains roughly 50 million solar masses of molecular gas at extremely high densities, temperatures, and turbulence. Despite seemingly favourable conditions for star formation, it forms stars at a surprisingly low rate, possibly suppressed by shear, strong magnetic fields, and turbulence driven by the galactic gravitational potential.

The Sun's convection zone extends from about 70% of the solar radius to the photosphere; within it, energy is transported outward by buoyant convective cells. Below it, in the radiative zone, energy diffuses outward as photons on a random walk lasting tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of years — whereas in the convection zone energy is carried by bulk fluid motions in only a few weeks.

TRAPPIST-1e is considered one of the most promising targets in the search for potentially habitable exoplanets — it is rocky, Earth-sized, and orbits within the conservative habitable zone of its ultra-cool red dwarf host star 40 light-years away. JWST is actively obtaining thermal emission and transmission spectra of the TRAPPIST-1 planets to determine whether any retain substantial atmospheres.

The Lockman Hole is a region of the sky in the constellation Ursa Major with the lowest known column density of neutral hydrogen in the Milky Way, allowing the clearest possible view of the extragalactic universe at ultraviolet and X-ray wavelengths. It is one of the most studied patches of sky for deep surveys of distant galaxies.

The rotation period of the Sun varies with latitude — a phenomenon called differential rotation. The equatorial regions rotate once every about 25 days, while polar regions rotate more slowly, taking about 35 days. This differential rotation stretches and distorts the Sun's magnetic field lines, eventually causing them to become tangled and erupt through the photosphere as sunspots and active regions.

The interstellar medium (ISM) in the Milky Way contains magnetic fields with a strength of a few microgauss permeating the diffuse gas. These fields are detected through Faraday rotation of polarised radio waves from background pulsars and quasars, and they play important roles in regulating star formation, accelerating cosmic rays, and supporting gas against gravitational collapse.

Black hole shadows — the dark region in the centre of the accretion disc images captured by the Event Horizon Telescope — are larger than the event horizon itself because the intense gravity bends light so strongly that photons on nearly circular paths form the bright photon ring around the shadow. The shadow diameter is 2.6 times the Schwarzschild diameter.

The Lyman-alpha forest is the series of absorption lines seen in the spectra of distant quasars, caused by neutral hydrogen clouds at many different redshifts along the line of sight each absorbing at the Lyman-alpha wavelength (121.6 nm) but appearing at different observed wavelengths due to their varying distances. It provides a powerful 3D map of the distribution of neutral gas in the early universe.

The Milky Way is currently accreting gas from several sources, including the Magellanic Stream and high-velocity clouds of gas raining down from the galactic halo. This gas accretion feeds continued star formation; without new gas the Milky Way would exhaust its current star-forming gas in roughly 2 billion years at its current star-formation rate.

RR Lyrae stars are a class of pulsating variable stars with pulsation periods of 0.2 to 1 day and luminosities nearly uniform at about 40–45 solar luminosities. Because they are old, metal-poor, and found in globular clusters and galaxy halos, they are used as distance indicators and tracers of old stellar populations across the galaxy and in nearby galaxies.

The Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is being torn apart by the Milky Way's tidal forces, and its material has been deposited in a stream that wraps around the sky. Remarkably, the Sun may contain some stars originally from Sagittarius — absorbed into the Milky Way disc through the ongoing merger process.

The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) detected the polarisation of the CMB, finding the characteristic E-mode patterns that confirmed the standard model of inflation. The Planck satellite subsequently detected B-mode polarisation from gravitational lensing and placed upper limits on primordial gravitational wave-induced B-modes, constraining the energy scale of inflation.

The first spacecraft to successfully land on and transmit data from another planet was the Soviet Venera 7, which touched down on Venus on December 15, 1970, and transmitted 23 minutes of data showing a surface temperature of about 475°C and pressure of about 90 atmospheres. The extreme conditions of Venus have destroyed every lander sent there within hours to days.

Radio pulsars lose rotational energy over time as they emit electromagnetic radiation and relativistic particles, causing their pulse period to gradually increase. The pulsar period derivative (dP/dt) gives an estimate of the pulsar's characteristic age (P/2Ṗ), spin-down luminosity, and surface magnetic field — properties that span an enormous range across the known pulsar population.

Galaxy bimodality describes the observed division of galaxies into two broad populations: blue, star-forming disc galaxies and red, quiescent elliptical galaxies, with relatively few in between (the 'green valley'). This bimodality arises because galaxies can transition from active to quiescent — through AGN feedback, mergers, or gas stripping — but do so relatively rapidly on cosmological timescales.

The Solar System's Hill sphere — the region around each planet where it dominates the gravitational attraction over the Sun — determines how far out a planet can hold onto moons. Earth's Hill sphere extends about 1.5 million kilometres, which is why the Moon at 384,400 km is safely within it, while the Lagrange L1 and L2 points (used by spacecraft like JWST) sit on the edge of this zone.

The double pulsar system PSR J0737-3039A/B, discovered in 2003, contains two active pulsars orbiting each other — the only known such system in the galaxy. Its extreme compactness and the precise timing of two pulsars have provided the most stringent tests of general relativity in strong-field conditions, confirming Einstein's predictions to 0.05% accuracy.

Cosmic reionisation ended the 'Dark Ages' of the universe — the period from about 380,000 to 400 million years after the Big Bang when no stars or galaxies yet existed to illuminate the neutral hydrogen fog. The light from the first stars gradually reionised the surrounding hydrogen, eventually completing by redshift z ~ 6, and the universe became transparent to ultraviolet radiation.

Epsilon Eridani, one of the closest Sun-like stars at only 10.5 light-years, has a prominent debris disc — the first extrasolar debris disc imaged — and at least one confirmed planet. Its young age (~800 million years, comparable to our solar system at the time of the Late Heavy Bombardment) makes it a natural laboratory for studying early planetary system evolution.

The orbital resonance between Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede — in a 1:2:4 pattern called the Laplace resonance — was probably established early in the solar system's history and is maintained by gravitational interactions. This resonance ensures that Io and Europa will always be in tidal flexing, maintaining Io's volcanism and Europa's subsurface ocean indefinitely into the future.

The Spitzer Space Telescope's detection in 2005 of atmospheric thermal emission from the hot Jupiter HD 209458b — directly measuring the contrast between the planet's day and night hemispheres — was the first direct detection of light from an exoplanet. This opened the field of exoplanet atmospheric characterisation decades before JWST made it routine.

Sgr A*'s mass of 4 million solar masses means its Schwarzschild radius is about 12 million kilometres — roughly 17 solar radii — making the event horizon a compact structure given the size of our galaxy. The 'shadow' imaged by the EHT in 2022 appears only 50 micro-arcseconds across as seen from Earth, equivalent to seeing an orange on the Moon.

Milky Way has over 200 known stellar streams — ribbons of stars sharing similar orbits that were once part of disrupted globular clusters or dwarf galaxies. The S1 stream discovered in 2018 is particularly notable because it may be associated with the dark matter 'debris flow' hypothesised to produce a localized density enhancement at the Sun's position relevant for dark matter direct detection experiments.

Photons are gravitationally deflected by massive objects, a prediction of general relativity first confirmed during the solar eclipse of May 29, 1919, by expeditions led by Arthur Eddington. Starlight passing near the Sun was deflected by 1.75 arcseconds — exactly double Newton's corpuscular prediction — making Einstein's general relativity the accepted theory of gravity.

The mass of the Milky Way is estimated at between 0.7 and 2 trillion solar masses within 100 kiloparsecs of the galactic centre, with the uncertainty dominated by the poorly constrained extent and mass of the dark matter halo. Satellite galaxy orbits, stellar stream kinematics from Gaia, and the escape velocity of stars with extreme velocities all provide independent estimates.

The Cherenkov light detected by ground-based gamma-ray observatories (MAGIC, VERITAS, H.E.S.S.) is produced when gamma-ray-induced electromagnetic particle showers develop in Earth's upper atmosphere, emitting a faint blue light cone for about 5 nanoseconds. The 'telescopes' are really large-aperture fast cameras imaging this fleeting atmospheric light, which allows reconstruction of the original gamma-ray's direction and energy.

The coldest known brown dwarf, WISE J085510.83-071442.5, has an effective temperature of approximately 225–260 K — colder than the boiling point of water and approaching the temperature of Earth's surface. It is only about 7.2 light-years away, making it one of the four nearest neighbours of the Sun.

The ecliptic plane contains all the major planets but is inclined about 60 degrees relative to the galactic plane — meaning the galaxy's plane is not aligned with the solar system's orbital plane. This inclination is the reason that the zodiacal light and the Milky Way appear as two separate bands crossing the night sky at a large angle.

The Chandrasekhar-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation of state for neutron stars includes contributions from neutron degeneracy pressure and repulsive nuclear forces at short range — but our poor knowledge of the repulsive nuclear interactions at supranuclear densities is the primary source of uncertainty in the neutron star equation of state. Gravitational wave observations of neutron star mergers from LIGO/Virgo are providing new constraints.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST survey will generate about 15 terabytes of raw image data per night — approximately 500 petabytes over its 10-year mission — creating the largest astronomical database ever assembled. Its automated alert system will generate millions of transient event alerts nightly for follow-up by other telescopes worldwide.

The Magellanic Bridge is a stream of gas and stars connecting the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, stretching about 43,000 light-years between them. It contains a population of young stars that formed within the bridge itself — unusually far from either galaxy — and traces the ongoing tidal interaction between the two clouds.

Binary stars — pairs of stars in gravitationally bound orbits — are thought to comprise roughly half of all stellar systems in the Milky Way. They are crucial laboratories for measuring stellar masses (through Kepler's third law applied to their orbital periods and separations) and for understanding phenomena like Type Ia supernovae, X-ray binaries, and millisecond pulsars.

Titan's methane hydrological cycle is driven by the slow evaporation of hydrocarbon lakes near the poles and precipitation back to the surface; modelling suggests this cycle has a timescale of roughly 1,000 years, far longer than Earth's water cycle. Titan's equatorial dunes, hundreds of metres tall and consisting of solid organic particles, suggest that winds transport material from polar regions to the equator over geological time.

The Einstein cross (Q2237+0305) is a gravitationally lensed quasar in which the background quasar is imaged as four distinct copies arranged in a cross pattern around the lensing foreground galaxy. Each of the four images shows the same quasar at slightly different times due to the different path lengths — allowing measurement of the Hubble constant through time-delay cosmography.

Neon — the second most abundant noble gas — is also the fifth most abundant element in the Sun and in the universe, produced primarily in massive stars via helium burning. Despite its cosmic abundance, neon is extraordinarily rare in Earth's atmosphere (less than 0.002%) because, being chemically inert, it was not incorporated into Earth's rocks during formation and instead escaped to space.

Titan's thick nitrogen atmosphere (1.5 times Earth's sea-level pressure at Titan's surface) has been compared to early Earth's atmosphere before the rise of free oxygen. The proposed Dragonfly rotorcraft lander mission, scheduled to arrive at Titan in the 2030s, will fly to dozens of sites to study its organic chemistry and potential prebiotic conditions.

The Breakthrough Starshot initiative, proposed in 2016, aims to develop laser-propelled light-sail spacecraft (StarChips) capable of reaching 20% of the speed of light — enough to reach Alpha Centauri in about 20 years. The key technological challenge is creating a gram-scale spacecraft that can survive the interstellar medium journey and transmit data over 4.2 light-years.

The Sun's activity cycle of approximately 11 years is actually the visible half of a 22-year magnetic cycle (Hale cycle): the polarity of the Sun's magnetic poles reverses with each 11-year activity cycle and returns to the original polarity after 22 years. This reversal is associated with the solar polar field reversal that occurs near each solar maximum.

The Doppler effect in astronomy allows not just radial velocity measurement of stars, but also the mapping of gas motions within galaxies and galaxy clusters. Integral field spectroscopy — simultaneously obtaining spectra at thousands of spatial positions — has transformed our understanding of stellar kinematics, gas flows, and AGN outflows within individual galaxies.

Neptune's Great Dark Spot, observed by Voyager 2 in 1989, was an anticyclonic storm system about the size of Earth. When the Hubble Space Telescope first observed Neptune in 1994, the spot had vanished — replaced by a new bright cloud system in the planet's northern hemisphere, suggesting that such storms on Neptune are much shorter-lived than Jupiter's Great Red Spot.

The solar system barycenter — the point around which all solar system bodies orbit — is sometimes inside the Sun but can be outside the Sun's surface when Jupiter and Saturn are on the same side of the Sun. The Sun itself wobbles around this barycenter by up to 1.5 solar radii over decades due to the gravitational influence of the giant planets.

Cataclysmic variable stars (CVs) are binary systems in which a white dwarf accretes material from a companion star that fills its Roche lobe — the teardrop-shaped region within which material is gravitationally bound to that star. Novae occur when the accreted hydrogen on the white dwarf surface undergoes runaway thermonuclear burning, producing a sudden brightening by 8–15 magnitudes visible to the naked eye.

The concept of stellar mass loss through winds was not well understood until it was confirmed by observations of P Cygni line profiles — spectral features showing simultaneous absorption at blue-shifted wavelengths and emission at the line centre — in the spectra of hot massive stars. These profile shapes are the diagnostic signature of an expanding shell of gas moving toward the observer.

Near-infrared surveys like 2MASS (Two Micron All Sky Survey) have been essential for mapping the stellar structure of the Milky Way because infrared light penetrates dust far better than visible light. The 2MASS survey detected over 470 million point sources and has been fundamental for identifying star clusters embedded in dark clouds, mapping the galactic bar, and charting the distribution of old stars.

Gravitational microlensing by stellar-mass black holes — where an isolated black hole passes in front of a background star — can be distinguished from ordinary stellar lensing because the event duration is longer and the lens itself emits no light. Astrometric microlensing using Hubble and Gaia measures the tiny positional shift of the background star, which combined with the light curve can constrain the lens mass.

The solar system's age of 4.568 billion years is known to within a few million years from radiometric dating of calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs) in primitive meteorites. CAIs are the oldest solid material in the solar system, condensed directly from the solar nebula, and their lead-lead isotope ratios provide the most precise absolute ages in geochronology.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) occur when a star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and is torn apart by tidal forces, producing a bright flare as about half the star's mass falls back and is accreted.
