TDEs are detected as sudden UV and X-ray brightening in the nuclei of otherwise quiescent galaxies and allow us to study accretion onto supermassive black holes in real time.

The cosmological constant Λ, originally introduced by Einstein in 1917 to make his equations compatible with a static universe, was abandoned by him after Hubble discovered the universe was expanding. It was reintroduced in 1998 when the accelerating expansion of the universe was discovered, and dark energy behaves observationally exactly like a positive cosmological constant.

The Fermi-LAT (Large Area Telescope) has detected gamma-ray emission from thousands of sources since its 2008 launch — the most productive high-energy survey in history. Among its discoveries are evidence that supernova remnants accelerate cosmic rays to very high energies, the Fermi Bubbles, and a population of gamma-ray emitting millisecond pulsars that have provided the first pulsar tests of general relativity.

Stars form in molecular clouds when a region of gas becomes gravitationally unstable and collapses — a process that takes about 100,000 years for a solar-mass protostar to form an accretion disc and begin deuterium burning. The protostellar accretion disc is the birthplace of planetary systems, with dust grains coagulating into pebbles, then planetesimals, then planetary embryos over millions of years.

Exoplanet atmospheric retrieval is the mathematical process of inferring atmospheric composition, temperature structure, and cloud properties from transmission or emission spectra. It involves fitting complex forward models of atmospheric radiative transfer — with hundreds of molecular opacity lines — to observed spectra using Bayesian statistical methods, and has become a core tool in the JWST exoplanet science programme.

The Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST) in China, the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, and Euclid are part of a new generation of wide-field survey facilities that together will map billions of galaxies across many epochs of cosmic history. Their combined datasets will provide overlapping, cross-calibrated probes of dark energy that are expected to reduce systematic uncertainties dramatically compared to individual surveys.

Substellar companions span a continuum from massive rocky planets through gas giants to brown dwarfs — with no sharp physical boundary separating them. The 'brown dwarf desert' — the observed scarcity of companions with masses between ~13 and ~80 Jupiter masses at orbital separations under 5 AU around solar-type stars — suggests that stellar-mass companions and planetary companions form through different mechanisms.

text: The first detection of an atmosphere on a rocky exoplanet was a major goal of JWST and was tentatively achieved with 55 Cancri e, a super-Earth whose JWST secondary eclipse spectroscopy in 2023 showed evidence for a volatile-rich atmosphere — possibly volcanic in origin. The atmospheric composition and volatile inventory of small rocky exoplanets are key discriminators between different formation scenarios.

Gravitational wave astronomy entered a new regime with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), approved by ESA for launch in 2035. LISA will detect millihertz gravitational waves — inaccessible to ground-based detectors because of seismic noise — from supermassive black hole mergers, compact binary systems throughout the galaxy, and possibly cosmological sources from the early universe.

Vesta, the second most massive body in the asteroid belt at 525 km diameter, has a giant impact basin at its south pole (Rheasilvia) 500 km across and 22 km deep — one of the largest impact craters in the solar system relative to body size. NASA's Dawn mission confirmed that Vesta has a differentiated interior with an iron-nickel core, making it more planet-like than most asteroids.

The BICEP/Keck programme at the South Pole observes the polarisation of the CMB at degree angular scales where primordial gravitational waves from inflation would leave a distinctive B-mode polarisation signature. Despite a false alarm in 2014 (contaminated by galactic dust), ongoing BICEP/Keck measurements have placed the tightest constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r, limiting the energy scale of inflation.

The 47 Tucanae globular cluster, visible to the naked eye in the southern hemisphere and lying about 16,700 light-years away, is one of the most massive globular clusters in the Milky Way with nearly 1 million stars. Its deep Hubble observations first measured the white dwarf cooling sequence, confirming a cluster age of about 11 billion years and setting constraints on the age of the universe.

The exoplanet K2-18b, a sub-Neptune orbiting in its host star's habitable zone 120 light-years away, showed tentative evidence for dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in its JWST transmission spectrum in 2023 — a compound that on Earth is produced exclusively by marine microorganisms. The detection was considered tentative rather than confirmed, requiring further observations to rule out non-biological chemistry.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) — networks of millisecond pulsars monitored for tiny variations in their pulse arrival times — have recently detected a stochastic background of low-frequency gravitational waves permeating the galaxy. The signals, simultaneously reported by IPTA, NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, and CPTA in 2023, are consistent with the background expected from millions of inspiralling supermassive black hole binaries throughout the universe.

The iron catastrophe was the early Earth event in which iron and other dense metals sank through the molten mantle to form the planet's core, releasing enormous heat that maintained the Earth in a partially molten state for hundreds of millions of years. This event is thought to have occurred within the first 30 million years after Earth's formation and created the conditions for Earth's protective magnetic field.

Astronomers divide the light from distant galaxies into red-shifts and blue-shifts to measure their recession and approach velocities. Edwin Hubble's 1929 discovery that galaxies are receding with velocities proportional to their distances — the Hubble-Lemaître law — provided the first observational evidence that the universe is expanding, a finding that revolutionised cosmology.

The Hawking radiation mechanism, proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974, predicts that black holes are not perfectly black but emit thermal radiation due to quantum effects near the event horizon. This process is so faint for stellar-mass black holes as to be undetectable, but it is theoretically important because it implies black holes eventually evaporate, raising profound questions about the fate of information that falls into them.

Pulsar recycling occurs when a neutron star in a binary system accretes material and angular momentum from a companion star, spinning up to millisecond rotation periods — producing a millisecond pulsar (MSP). MSPs can rotate hundreds of times per second and are extraordinarily stable clocks, more accurate than atomic clocks, enabling precision tests of general relativity and gravitational wave detection.

The most detailed image of the surface of a star other than the Sun was obtained by GRAVITY and MATISSE instruments on the VLTI for the red supergiant star Antares, revealing a turbulent surface with large convective cells and an extended chromosphere. This level of detail was achieved by combining the light from four 8-metre Unit Telescopes using optical interferometry with a baseline of 130 metres.

Hypervelocity stars have been accelerated to velocities exceeding the Milky Way's escape speed (typically 500–700 km/s at the Sun's distance from the centre) by the Hills mechanism — a close encounter of a binary star with the galactic centre's supermassive black hole, which captures one star while flinging the other out at extreme velocity. Nearly 30 hypervelocity stars have been confirmed, all traced back to Sgr A*.

The sunspot cycle's 11-year period was discovered by Heinrich Schwabe in 1843 after 17 years of observing sunspot counts. The number of sunspots is tracked by the Sunspot Number, a standard index dating back to 1749, making the solar cycle the longest continuously monitored astrophysical cycle in history.

JWST's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam) has detected galaxies at redshifts above z = 13 — corresponding to epochs less than 320 million years after the Big Bang — that are brighter and more numerous than standard galaxy formation models predicted. These early bright galaxies challenge our understanding of how quickly the first stars and galaxies could form and grow.

The solar neighbourhood within 10 parsecs of the Sun contains about 350 known stellar systems (including multi-star systems). Red dwarfs (M-type stars) make up the vast majority — roughly 70% of all stars in the galaxy — but are too faint to be seen without binoculars from Earth, meaning our naked-eye perception of the night sky is completely dominated by rare bright massive stars.

The Cosmic Infrared Background Explorer mission (CIBER) measured diffuse near-infrared background fluctuations that exceeded what could be accounted for by known galaxy populations, suggesting an additional component of emission — possibly from intracluster stars stripped from galaxies or from Population III stars at very high redshifts. The origin of this excess remains a topic of active debate.

The velocity dispersion of stars in a galaxy's bulge or elliptical galaxy's central region scales tightly with the mass of the central supermassive black hole — the M-sigma relation. This tight correlation suggests that black hole growth and the surrounding galaxy's growth are causally linked through feedback processes, despite the black hole's sphere of gravitational influence being vastly smaller than the galaxy.

The Chandra Deep Field South is one of the deepest X-ray images ever taken — a total of over 7 million seconds (about 80 days) of Chandra observation accumulated over many years. It revealed that virtually every faint X-ray source in the distant universe is an AGN, showing that black hole accretion was far more common in the early universe when gas supplies were more plentiful.

The Moon's albedo — its reflectivity — is only about 12%, making it roughly as reflective as asphalt, despite appearing brilliantly bright in the night sky. This dark surface is coloured by space weathering: bombardment by micrometeorites and solar wind ions that gradually reddened and darkened the initially brighter anorthosite crust over billions of years.

The Milky Way's outer disc flare — where the disc thickness increases dramatically beyond about 40,000 light-years from the galactic centre — reaches a scale height of about 5,000 light-years at 65,000 light-years from the centre. This flare may be caused by the gravitational interaction with the Magellanic Clouds or by the gradually decreasing gravitational restoring force as the dark matter halo's density drops off.

The Fermi-GBT (Gamma-ray Burst Monitor) on the Fermi satellite detects a gamma-ray burst somewhere in the sky approximately once per day, probing the full sky continuously for transient events from microbursts to short and long GRBs. It has observed terrestrial gamma-ray flashes — intense bursts of gamma rays produced by thunderstorms in Earth's atmosphere — confirming that energetic particle acceleration occurs during lightning.

The solar system's age can also be independently inferred by studying the stellar population of the Milky Way's thin disc: the distribution of stellar ages inferred from isochrone fitting and asteroseismology shows the Sun formed near the peak of the disc's star-formation activity about 4.6 billion years ago. Our solar system is neither unusually young nor old for a Milky Way thin disc stellar system.

The total number of galaxies in the observable universe was revised upward in 2016 using Hubble Deep Field data combined with modelling of galaxies too small and faint to detect even with Hubble; the revised estimate is about 2 trillion galaxies, roughly 10 times the previous estimate of 200 billion. Most of these 2 trillion galaxies are intrinsically small, faint dwarf galaxies in the distant universe that are currently beyond detection.

The stellar black hole candidate Cygnus X-1 was one of the first evidence-backed black holes, identified in 1971 when X-ray observations from Uhuru showed it was orbiting an unseen companion with mass clearly above the neutron star limit. Stephen Hawking famously made a bet in 1974 that it was not a black hole — a bet he conceded in 1990 when the evidence became overwhelming.

Stellar seismology is now used as a clock for stellar ages through main-sequence turnoff points in clusters: the more massive stars at the tip of the main sequence have evolved fastest, and the luminosity at which stars begin to evolve off the main sequence (the turnoff point) depends sensitively on the cluster's age. This technique has confirmed the age of the universe is at least 13.4 billion years based on the oldest globular cluster ages.

The active asteroid (3200) Phaethon — progenitor of the Geminid meteor shower — is a member of the rare class of 'rock comet' that exhibits cometary-like activity (a short dust tail near perihelion) but is compositionally an asteroid, not an ice-rich comet. Japan's DESTINY+ mission, scheduled for launch around 2025–2028, aims to fly past Phaethon and image its surface.

The mass-metallicity relation shows that more massive galaxies contain stars with higher average heavy-element abundance (metallicity). This arises because massive galaxies have deeper gravitational potential wells that retain the heavy elements ejected by supernova explosions, while low-mass galaxies lose their metals in galactic winds, enriching the circumgalactic and intergalactic medium.

The Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), launched in 2010, continuously monitors the Sun at 10 different UV and EUV wavelengths and sends back about 1.5 terabytes of data per day — more data than any previous NASA mission. Its high-cadence, high-resolution imagery has revealed a solar atmosphere far more dynamic and structured than previously known, with countless small impulsive energy release events.

Supernova 1987A — the closest naked-eye supernova since 1604 — exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud on February 23, 1987, and was detected in multiple messenger channels: 24 neutrinos were detected in terrestrial underground detectors hours before the optical brightening reached Earth, confirming the core-collapse model. Astronomers have been watching the remnant grow and brighten as the supernova ejecta ploughs into a pre-existing circumstellar ring.

Galactic archaeology uses the chemical and kinematic properties of stars as 'fossils' to reconstruct the Milky Way's history. The field of chemical evolution modelling tracks how successive generations of star formation and supernova enrichment gradually built up the galaxy's metallicity from near zero to the solar value over 10 billion years.

The Wilsons Observatory on Mount Wilson, California, has been central to several pivotal discoveries in astronomy: Hubble confirmed the extragalactic nature of spiral nebulae there using the 100-inch Hooker Telescope in 1923, and Penzias and Wilson's detection of the CMB was confirmed using a 20-foot horn antenna in New Jersey. Today, the Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy (CHARA) interferometric array on Mount Wilson achieves the highest angular resolution of any optical telescope.

The first interstellar molecule identified by radio astronomy was hydroxyl (OH) at 1667 MHz, detected in 1963. Since then, radio spectroscopy has identified over 200 molecular species in the ISM, including complex organics with 12 or more atoms such as propyl cyanide and the sugar-related molecule glycolaldehyde. These discoveries suggest that cosmic chemistry is far richer than previously imagined.

The concept of gravitational waves carrying energy was a subject of controversy even among relativists for decades after Einstein's 1916 prediction. The question of whether gravitational waves are real physical phenomena or coordinate artefacts was not definitively settled until the 1950s–1960s work of Bondi, Pirani, and others, and was confirmed experimentally only by the binary pulsar timing of Hulse and Taylor in the 1970s.

The Hubble Ultra Deep Field (HUDF), released in 2004, revealed about 10,000 galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length — a region previously thought to be essentially empty. Its successor, the eXtreme Deep Field (XDF, 2012), combined 2 million seconds of Hubble exposures to reveal galaxies up to 13.2 billion light-years away.

The Psyche asteroid, target of NASA's Psyche mission (launched 2023, arrival expected ~2029), is unique because it may be the exposed iron-nickel metallic core of a differentiated planetesimal whose rocky mantle was stripped by collisions in the early solar system. If so, it would provide a direct look at the kind of material forming the core of rocky planets like Earth, which is otherwise inaccessible.

The Venus zone — the orbital region inside the habitable zone where a planet like Venus would undergo a runaway greenhouse effect — is thought to be inhabited by exoplanets with dense CO2 atmospheres that trap heat beyond the point of habitability. Several of the TRAPPIST-1 planets lie in or near this zone, motivating JWST observations to determine if they resemble Earth or Venus.

The cosmic microwave background's power spectrum — a plot of temperature fluctuation amplitude versus angular scale — shows a series of acoustic peaks corresponding to the fundamental frequency and harmonics of oscillating baryonic plasma in the early universe. The positions and heights of these peaks precisely encode the cosmological parameters, including the total density of matter, dark energy, and baryons.

Astronomers discovered in 2021 that Sgr A*'s accretion disc occasionally flares dramatically in near-infrared and X-rays for tens of minutes, with the brightest flares having luminosities thousands of times greater than the quiescent state. These flares may result from magnetic reconnection events accelerating plasma to near-relativistic speeds just outside the event horizon.

The Hot Big Bang model is supported by four key observational pillars: the expansion of the universe (Hubble-Lemaître law), the cosmic microwave background radiation, the abundance of light elements from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and the large-scale structure of the universe consistent with primordial density perturbations. Together these independent lines of evidence make the Big Bang the best-supported theory in cosmology.

The gamma-ray binary LS I +61 303 consists of a Be star and a compact object (possibly a pulsar or black hole) in an eccentric 26.5-day orbit, producing spectacular periodic radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray flares near periastron. Its high-energy emission — detected up to 25 TeV by MAGIC and VERITAS — makes it one of a small number of known gamma-ray binaries and a laboratory for studying particle acceleration in compact object environments.

Light pollution has reduced the visibility of the Milky Way for more than one-third of the world's population and over 99% of people in the United States and Europe. The Globe at Night programme, coordinated by NOIRLab, engages citizen scientists worldwide in monitoring light pollution by counting visible stars in standard constellations — creating a decades-long dataset showing the ongoing loss of dark skies.

The Milky Way's magnetic field is roughly 5–10 microgauss in the disc and has a large-scale spiral structure that may trace the galaxy's spiral arms, along with turbulent small-scale fluctuations. The field is measured through the synchrotron emission of relativistic electrons spiralling along field lines and through Faraday rotation of polarised radio signals from pulsars and background galaxies.

text: Photon pressure — radiation pressure — plays a crucial role in the evolution of massive stars and in driving winds off their surfaces. For the most massive stars, radiation pressure on opacity is so strong that it actually limits how massive a star can form: the Eddington luminosity is the luminosity at which radiation pressure exactly balances gravity, and stars near this limit shed mass catastrophically.

The Kuiper Belt object Quaoar, roughly 1,100 km in diameter, was found in 2023 to have a ring system at a distance twice as large as Roche limit predictions — the distance at which ring material should coalesce into a moon — suggesting its ring material is too cold and elastic to clump. This discovery challenged existing theories about ring formation and stability.

The galactic centre region is one of the most complex and extreme environments in the Milky Way, containing the nuclear star cluster (the densest collection of stars in the galaxy), the circumnuclear disc (a ring of molecular gas around Sgr A*), the Sgr A complex of gas and dust, and an assortment of puzzling objects like the G objects — compact dusty gas clouds with orbits suggesting they may be merged stellar binaries.

Omega Centauri is thought to contain an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) of 8,000 to 50,000 solar masses at its centre, based on stellar velocity dispersions and X-ray emission. IMBHs — with masses between stellar-mass black holes (~3-100 solar masses) and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) — have been elusive, and Omega Centauri remains one of the best candidates for hosting one.

Methanol masers associated with forming high-mass stars are used as tracers of early star formation and as part of VLBI parallax measurements that have directly mapped the three-dimensional spiral arm structure of the Milky Way. The BeSSeL survey has measured trigonometric parallaxes to hundreds of masers in star-forming regions, providing a detailed picture of our galaxy's spiral structure from within.

The solar neutrino problem — the observed deficit of solar electron neutrinos compared to theoretical predictions — was resolved by the discovery of neutrino oscillations, showing that neutrinos change flavour as they propagate. The SNO (Sudbury Neutrino Observatory) experiment in 2001 measured the total flux of all neutrino flavours from the Sun and found it matched the solar model precisely, confirming both neutrino oscillations and the proton-proton chain solar model.

Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko — Rosetta's target — has a shape like a rubber duck because two separately formed lobes gently collided and merged in the early solar system. Its composition includes water ice, carbon dioxide, organic molecules, and even molecular oxygen (O2) — an unexpected discovery, since O2 reacts readily and should have been destroyed long ago.

The Zeeman effect — the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of a magnetic field — allows direct measurement of magnetic field strengths in astrophysical plasmas from spectropolarimetry. In molecular clouds, Zeeman splitting of the 21-cm hydrogen line and OH/CN molecular lines has revealed magnetic field strengths of a few to tens of microgauss — suggesting magnetic fields are important in supporting clouds against gravitational collapse.

Jupiter's moon Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in the solar system, its ancient ice-rock surface preserving a complete record of the early bombardment history of the outer solar system. Unlike the other Galilean moons, Callisto shows no evidence of internal differentiation — its rock and ice appear to be uniformly mixed throughout — possibly because it formed slowly and never heated enough to separate.

The stellar luminosity function — the number of stars per unit volume at each luminosity — has been measured in the solar neighbourhood and shows that low-luminosity M dwarfs vastly outnumber more luminous stars. Despite being 1,000 times more numerous than the Sun, the total contribution of M dwarfs to the galaxy's luminosity is only about 2% because each individual M dwarf is so dim.

The Curiosity rover's methane measurements on Mars caused considerable excitement when seasonal variations in atmospheric methane were detected — a possible sign of geological or biological processes. However, the ESA Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) found no methane when it began monitoring Mars's atmosphere in 2018, creating a discrepancy that has not been fully resolved and remains one of Mars science's most intriguing open questions.

The AGB (asymptotic giant branch) thermal pulse phase occurs when a low-mass star alternates between hydrogen and helium shell burning, producing periodic bursts of nuclear energy that cause dredge-up events mixing freshly synthesised carbon and s-process elements from the interior to the stellar surface. This is how carbon stars form: AGB stars that have dredged up so much carbon that their carbon-to-oxygen ratio exceeds one.

Dwarf irregular galaxies — small, gas-rich galaxies with no regular structure — are among the least chemically evolved systems in the universe, with metallicities sometimes less than 1/50th of the solar value. I Zwicky 18, with a metallicity only about 1/50th solar, was long considered a candidate for a truly primordial galaxy forming stars for the first time, though subsequent deep observations found older underlying stellar populations.

The tidal tail of Sagittarius Dwarf galaxy has been found to contain a significant number of RR Lyrae stars and other old stellar tracers that can be used to measure the Milky Way's gravitational potential as a function of radius. These tracers, spread over the sky, provide constraints on dark matter density profiles that no single observation from one location could provide.

Chandra observed the X-ray afterglow of GW170817's neutron star merger, detecting a jet of X-ray emission that grew steadily brighter over months before fading. This was the first direct evidence that short gamma-ray bursts produce structured, collimated jets, and the geometry of the jet — slightly off-axis as seen from Earth — was consistent with the weaker-than-average gamma-ray burst observed coincidentally with the gravitational wave signal.

Geomagnetic reversals — when Earth's magnetic poles swap positions — occur at irregular intervals averaging a few hundred thousand years, though the last reversal was about 780,000 years ago (the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal). During a reversal, which takes a few thousand to tens of thousands of years, the field weakens substantially, potentially allowing more cosmic rays to reach Earth's surface.

The total energy released by the Sun in its 10-billion-year lifetime is equivalent to about 4 × 10^50 joules, all derived from converting about 4% of its initial hydrogen mass (0.04 × 2 × 10^30 kg) into energy. This staggeringly large total energy output is nonetheless only about 1/5,000th the energy released by a core-collapse supernova in just a few seconds.

Star-forming regions often produce multiple stellar generations in rapid succession: the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from the first generation of massive stars compress nearby gas clouds, triggering the formation of a second generation of stars — a process called triggered star formation. The famous Eagle Nebula's Pillars of Creation are thought to be an example of this process.

The Sirius binary system — consisting of Sirius A (the brightest star in the sky) and Sirius B (the first white dwarf ever identified) — demonstrates how dramatically two stars in the same system can differ. Sirius A is twice the Sun's mass and 25 times as luminous, while Sirius B — originally more massive — has already evolved off the main sequence and shed its outer layers, leaving a compact white dwarf remnant.

The abundance of lithium in the oldest, most metal-poor stars in the Milky Way halo is remarkably constant — about a factor of three below the lithium abundance predicted by standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis — a discrepancy called the cosmological lithium problem. Proposed solutions include stellar depletion mechanisms, non-standard BBN physics, or new particle physics, but none is fully accepted.

Europa Clipper, NASA's mission to Jupiter's moon Europa launched in October 2024, will make nearly 50 close flybys of Europa during its prime mission, sampling its ice shell, subsurface ocean, and the plumes venting from the surface. Its suite of instruments — including an ice-penetrating radar — will characterise the ocean depth, ice shell thickness, and habitability potential with unprecedented detail.

Microquasars are X-ray binary systems that produce relativistic jets visible in radio waves — scaled-down versions of quasar jets driven by stellar-mass rather than supermassive black holes. Studying microquasars like SS 433 and GRS 1915+105 at close range in our own galaxy provides insights into the physics of accretion and jet formation that would take years to observe at quasar distances.

The Sun's magnetic activity cycle has been linked to changes in its total irradiance of about 0.1%, its UV output by about 10%, and its X-ray output by orders of magnitude. These changes affect Earth's stratospheric ozone chemistry, with potential knock-on effects on tropospheric circulation, though quantifying the climate signal precisely remains a challenging area of research.

The discovery that distant Type Ia supernovae were dimmer than expected (1998) implied they were farther away than a decelerating universe would produce — meaning the expansion is accelerating. This finding required either a cosmological constant, a new form of dark energy, or a modification of general relativity on cosmic scales, and remains one of the most profound unresolved questions in fundamental physics.

The photometric standard star network — a set of well-calibrated reference stars distributed across the sky — allows ground-based photometry to be tied to a common, absolute flux scale. Modern all-sky spectrophotometric surveys using white dwarf standard stars are pushing calibration accuracy to the 1% level, required for next-generation cosmological surveys to achieve their precision dark energy measurements.

Saturn's moon Mimas — famous for its large Herschel Crater giving it the appearance of the Death Star from Star Wars — may harbour a young, global subsurface liquid water ocean discovered through analysis of Cassini orbital data. The discovery, published in 2024, was unexpected as Mimas's cratered, ancient surface showed no geological signs of internal heat.

The galactic fountain model describes how supernova-driven hot gas rises from the galactic disc into the halo, cools, and rains back down as clouds of gas — replenishing the disc with gas that was enriched by the supernova explosions. This cycling of gas between disc and halo over timescales of tens to hundreds of millions of years is thought to be essential for sustaining star formation across the Milky Way.

Stars in binary systems sometimes transfer mass from the donor (the more evolved star whose outer layers overflow its Roche lobe) to the accretor, fundamentally altering the evolution of both stars. This mass transfer can spin up the accretor to rapid rotation, increase its luminosity, and in extreme cases produce novae, Type Ia supernovae, or millisecond pulsars — phenomena that would not occur in isolated single-star evolution.

The James Webb Space Telescope's NIRSpec microshutter array contains 250,000 individually addressable microscopic shutters — each the size of a grain of sand — that can be opened or closed to simultaneously observe up to 100 astronomical targets in a single field of view. This technology, developed by NASA Goddard, enables highly efficient spectroscopic surveys of galaxy populations at cosmic distances.

The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves in the millihertz band by using three spacecraft flying in an equilateral triangle formation with 2.5 million kilometre-long arms, trailing Earth in its orbit. Unlike ground-based detectors limited by seismic noise below ~10 Hz, LISA's space environment allows sensitivity at the much lower frequencies produced by supermassive black hole mergers.

Astronomical seeing — the blurring of starlight by atmospheric turbulence — is quantified by the size of a star's image (seeing disc) measured in arcseconds. The best sites in the world (Mauna Kea, Atacama) achieve median seeing of about 0.5–0.7 arcseconds; without adaptive optics, this limits angular resolution regardless of telescope size, which is why space telescopes offer such dramatic improvements.

Planet Nine — a hypothetical ninth planet in the outer solar system — has been proposed to explain a clustering of orbital elements seen in extreme trans-Neptunian objects. If it exists, it would be a planet of 5–10 Earth masses orbiting at ~400–800 AU with an orbital period of 10,000–20,000 years. Despite dedicated searches, no direct detection has been made, and the clustering could also be a statistical artefact.

Luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) emit most of their energy in the far-infrared due to intense star formation (or AGN activity) deeply embedded in dust that absorbs UV light and re-emits it thermally. ULIRGs (ultra-luminous infrared galaxies) are among the most intensely star-forming objects in the local universe, often created by major galaxy mergers and producing new stars at rates hundreds of times higher than the Milky Way.

Saturn's largest ring, the E ring, is exceptionally diffuse and extends from the orbit of Mimas to beyond Titan's orbit. Unlike Saturn's dense inner rings, the E ring is replenished by water ice particles from Enceladus's geysers, making it the largest known dynamically sustained ring in the solar system and a direct indicator of Enceladus's ongoing geologic activity.

Astronomical twilight — the period after sunset before the sky is fully dark — is classified into three types: civil (Sun between 0° and 6° below horizon), nautical (6° to 12°), and astronomical (12° to 18°). True astronomical darkness begins when the Sun is more than 18° below the horizon, which is when the sky is sufficiently dark for the faintest deep-sky observations.

The Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (PSR B1913+16), discovered in 1974, provided the first indirect evidence for gravitational wave emission: the two neutron stars are spiralling together at exactly the rate predicted by general relativity as energy is radiated away as gravitational waves. Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery.

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) — the hot, diffuse gas extending from the edges of a galaxy's disc out to its virial radius (the radius within which the dark matter halo is virialized) — contains a significant fraction of the galaxy's total baryonic mass and regulates gas inflow and outflow. COS/Hubble absorption line studies have detected metals extending over 300 kiloparsecs around nearby galaxies, far beyond their visible extent.

Black hole spin — described by a dimensionless parameter 'a' from 0 (non-rotating Schwarzschild) to 1 (maximally rotating Kerr) — affects the efficiency of energy extraction from infalling matter. A maximally spinning black hole can in principle convert up to 42% of infalling mass to energy (compared to ~6% for a Schwarzschild black hole), making highly spinning AGN the most efficient energy sources in the universe.

The Alpha Centauri system — the closest star system to the Sun at 4.37 light-years — consists of three stars: the binary pair Alpha Centauri A and B (which are Sun-like stars separated by about 23 AU) and the red dwarf Proxima Centauri (which at 4.24 light-years is the nearest individual star and may or may not be gravitationally bound to the AB pair). Proxima Centauri hosts at least one rocky planet, Proxima b.

The detection of exoplanet water vapour absorption features using Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 — first clearly achieved for the hot Jupiter HD 189733b in 2013 — opened the era of exoplanet atmospheric characterisation using space telescopes. The same planet is now routinely studied with JWST, which has detected sodium, potassium, and water features with far greater precision.

The diffuse gamma-ray background — the isotropic gamma-ray emission detected by Fermi after subtracting known discrete sources and galactic emission — is thought to originate primarily from unresolved blazars beyond the sensitivity of current surveys. A small fraction may arise from annihilation of dark matter particles, making precise measurement of its spectrum and anisotropy an important indirect dark matter search.

The Hayabusa2 mission (JAXA) returned samples from the carbonaceous asteroid Ryugu in December 2020 — finding organic matter, amino acids including all 20 proteinogenic amino acids, and liquid water inclusions in the samples. This confirmed that the building blocks of life can form in space and be delivered to planets via asteroidal impacts.

The Milky Way's thick disk, thin disc, stellar halo, and dark matter halo all extend to different radii and have different density profiles. Chemical tagging using the detailed abundance patterns of individual stars — now achievable at scale through spectroscopic surveys like GALAH, APOGEE, and Gaia-ESO — is allowing astronomers to trace individual stellar birth clusters across the whole galaxy.

The OSIRIS-REx mission, renamed OSIRIS-APEX after its asteroid Bennu sample return, is now heading to the near-Earth asteroid Apophis — which will make a historically close approach to Earth (within 32,000 km — inside geostationary orbit) on April 13, 2029. OSIRIS-APEX will arrive at Apophis shortly after closest approach to study how Earth's tidal forces alter the asteroid's spin, shape, and surface.

The solar wind termination shock, where the solar wind slows from supersonic to subsonic speeds before reaching the heliopause, was crossed outbound by Voyager 1 in 2004 at about 94 AU and Voyager 2 in 2007 at about 84 AU. The asymmetry in these crossing distances suggests the heliosphere is compressed on one side by the local interstellar medium flowing past.

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) — complex ring-structured organic molecules containing carbon and hydrogen — are among the most abundant molecules in the interstellar medium and emit characteristic infrared emission features at 3.3, 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, and 11.2 microns. These 'unidentified infrared bands' were a mystery for decades and are used to trace star-forming activity in galaxies across cosmic time.

The first space probe to reach interstellar space was Voyager 1 in 2012, as defined by the crossing of the heliopause. Yet our solar system's gravitational influence — through the Oort Cloud — extends far further, to roughly 100,000 AU (1.6 light-years). Voyager 1 will not exit the Oort Cloud for another 300 years at its current speed of about 17 km/s.

Galaxy harassment is a process whereby high-speed gravitational encounters between galaxies in dense cluster environments tidally distort and strip stars and gas from smaller galaxies, gradually transforming late-type spirals into lenticular (S0) or elliptical galaxies over many cluster crossing times. It is one of several environmental processes — alongside ram-pressure stripping and strangulation — that quench star formation in cluster galaxies.

The Sun's interior structure was verified by helioseismology: the sound speed profile determined from millions of oscillation modes agreed with solar models to better than 0.3% throughout most of the interior, providing one of the most precise tests of stellar physics. Only near the base of the convection zone, where the tachocline sits, is there a slight discrepancy possibly related to heavy element settling and diffusion.

The Huygens probe, released by Cassini, descended through Titan's atmosphere on January 14, 2005, in the most distant landing ever achieved at the time — and transmitted data for 72 minutes on the surface before its batteries died. It found a landscape shaped by liquid methane flows, rounded pebbles of water ice sculpted by hydrocarbon currents, and a thin mist extending kilometres above.

The Subaru Telescope's Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC), a 870-megapixel camera with a 1.5-degree field of view, has conducted the HSC Subaru Strategic Program — a 330-night, multi-band imaging survey covering 1,400 square degrees. Its weak lensing shear maps have provided independent cosmological constraints in tension with the Planck CMB measurements, contributing to the S8 tension that parallels the Hubble tension.

The Galactic All-sky Survey (GASS) mapped neutral hydrogen emission (21-cm) across the entire Southern sky at high velocity resolution, revealing the complex multi-phase structure of the Milky Way's gas: warm neutral medium, cold neutral medium, and diffuse ionised gas coexist and interact throughout the disc and halo. Similar northern surveys (EBHIS, CGPS) complete a full-sky picture of hydrogen in the Milky Way.

The zodiac sign Scorpius contains the brightest X-ray source in the sky outside our solar system — Scorpius X-1, the first X-ray source discovered beyond the Sun (1962). It is a neutron star in a low-mass X-ray binary accreting from a companion star and emits X-ray luminosity near its Eddington limit, continuously at a rate that would vaporise the Earth if it were as close as the Sun.

The cosmic web's filaments contain the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) at temperatures between 10^5 and 10^7 K — making them invisible to optical telescopes and detectable only in UV and X-ray absorption. Detecting the WHIM has been a major observational challenge; FRB dispersion measures provide independent estimates of its density and distribution that complement UV and X-ray observations.

The International Space Station orbits Earth at approximately 400 km altitude travelling at about 7.7 km/s, completing 15.5 orbits per day. Due to orbital velocity time dilation and gravitational time dilation, astronauts aboard ISS age about 0.007 seconds less per year than people on Earth — a tiny but measurable general and special relativistic effect confirmed by precision atomic clocks.

Gravitational lensing of the CMB by large-scale structure (CMB lensing) distorts the CMB temperature and polarisation patterns, providing a direct tracer of the total projected mass distribution along the line of sight. CMB lensing measurements from Planck, ACT, and SPT have been used to measure the growth of cosmic structure and are in mild tension with measurements from galaxy surveys (the S8 tension).

The Milky Way's central bulge is dominated by old stars that formed over 10 billion years ago during an early phase of rapid galactic growth, though a younger population (~1 billion years) also exists. Bulge stars show a range of metallicities and a distinctive bimodal velocity ellipsoid consistent with a peanut-shaped or X-shaped bulge structure — the product of bar buckling instability in the thin disc.

Ganymede has the largest ocean of any moon in the solar system — an internal saltwater ocean potentially containing more water than all Earth's oceans combined, sandwiched between layers of ice at depths of 150–250 km. Its existence was inferred from Hubble observations of its auroral activity, which would be damped by a conducting saline ocean interacting with Jupiter's magnetic field.

The 'Wow!' signal, detected by astronomer Jerry Ehman at Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope on August 15, 1977, was a strong narrowband signal at 1420 MHz lasting 72 seconds that has never been explained or repeated. It remains the most intriguing candidate for an artificial extraterrestrial signal ever detected, though most researchers consider a natural origin more likely.

Retrograde motion of outer planets — their apparent backwards movement against the background stars for a period each year — was puzzling to ancient astronomers and led to complex Ptolemaic epicycles to explain it. Copernicus showed it arises naturally because Earth overtakes the slower outer planets in their orbits, creating an optical illusion of backward motion without any change in the planet's actual direction of travel.

WISE J104915.57-531906.1, better known as Luhman 16, is a binary brown dwarf system only 6.52 light-years from Earth — the third nearest known system to the Sun. The two components, of spectral types L7.5 and T0.5, were discovered only in 2013 despite being so close, demonstrating how many cool objects in the solar neighbourhood may still await discovery.

Stellar activity on M dwarfs — including large X-ray flares, coronal mass ejections, and intense UV radiation — poses a significant threat to the habitability of their planets even when those planets orbit within the habitable zone. TRAPPIST-1 generates superflares far more powerful than the Sun's flares, and whether its habitable zone planets retain atmospheres is one of the most pressing questions in exoplanet science.

Deep impact craters on the Moon preserve in their central peaks rocks from deep within the lunar crust that were uplifted by the impact — allowing geologists to sample stratigraphy that would otherwise be inaccessible. The Tycho crater's central peak, probed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, contains olivine and pyroxene from depths of tens of kilometres.

The Gaia spacecraft's on-board focal plane contains 106 CCDs and 938 million pixels, making it the largest digital camera ever flown in space at the time of launch. It measures stellar positions to an accuracy of 7 micro-arcseconds for the brightest stars — equivalent to measuring the diameter of a human hair at the distance of the Moon.

Infrared spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres has detected carbon dioxide (CO2) at 4.3 microns in the atmosphere of WASP-39b using JWST in 2022 — the first unambiguous detection of CO2 in an exoplanet atmosphere. CO2 is a potential biosignature when combined with other molecules, and its detection validates JWST's capability to characterise Earth-like atmospheres in the coming decade.

Spiral galaxy M74 (NGC 628), a grand-design face-on spiral about 32 million light-years away, is particularly valued as a 'Rosetta Stone' for studying spiral structure because of its nearly circular disc geometry and well-defined spiral arms. JWST's mid-infrared imaging in 2022 revealed its spiral arms outlined by glowing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission and hot dust heated by young star-forming regions.

The Antarctic submillimetre telescopes at the South Pole — including the South Pole Telescope and BICEP array — benefit from the extremely dry, stable atmosphere at this location, where the precipitable water vapour column is the lowest on Earth. The geographic south pole also allows continuous viewing of a specific patch of sky as Earth rotates, ideal for CMB experiments requiring long integration times.

The Milky Way's open clusters — loose associations of a few hundred to a few thousand stars born from the same molecular cloud — gradually disperse as orbital perturbations and galactic tidal forces scatter their members. The Pleiades will disperse in about 250 million years; the Hyades cluster (the nearest open cluster at 153 light-years) is already past middle age at ~625 million years and has lost half its mass to evaporation.

Tectonic plate motion on Earth is partly driven by heat from the primordial formation of the planet and partly from ongoing radioactive decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the mantle. This combination of heat sources produces the mantle convection that drives plates at speeds of a few centimetres per year and has recycled Earth's crust repeatedly — erasing most of the surface record of the first billion years.

The Vela pulsar, the brightest pulsar in X-rays and one of the fastest-moving isolated neutron stars, was given a kick velocity of about 430 km/s when its progenitor star exploded as a supernova about 11,000 years ago. Such high pulsar kick velocities — some pulsars exceed 1,000 km/s — are thought to be imparted by asymmetries in the supernova explosion, though the exact mechanism remains debated.

The dark matter distribution in the Milky Way is described by a density profile that rises toward the galactic centre — whether as a 'cusp' (rising as ρ ∝ r^-1 as in NFW profiles from simulations) or 'core' (flattening to a constant density at the centre as seen in some dwarf galaxies) remains the 'core-cusp' problem of dark matter physics. Milky Way data currently favour a cored or adiabatically contracted NFW profile.

The origin of the Moon is explained by the Giant Impact Hypothesis: a Mars-sized protoplanet named Theia collided with the proto-Earth about 4.5 billion years ago, and the debris from this cataclysm coalesced in Earth's orbit to form the Moon. Evidence includes the Moon's similar oxygen isotope composition to Earth (unlike most solar system bodies), its low iron content, and the Earth-Moon system's high total angular momentum.

The Crab Nebula — one of the most studied objects in the sky — is the remnant of the supernova of 1054 AD and now extends about 11 light-years across, expanding at roughly 1,500 km/s. Its central pulsar dumps about 5 × 10^38 ergs per second into the nebula as relativistic electrons and magnetic fields, making the entire nebula a pulsar wind nebula that glows across the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays.

Spectroscopic binaries — binary star systems identified by periodic Doppler shifts in their spectra rather than by direct resolution of two stars — are far more numerous than visually resolved pairs because most binaries are too close together and too distant to separate optically. By measuring the orbital velocities and periods of both components (double-lined spectroscopic binaries), astronomers can derive the ratio of stellar masses.

The first detection of exoplanet weather — day-night temperature contrast and wind patterns — was made using phase curve observations that tracked the infrared brightness of a hot Jupiter as it orbited its star. For HD 189733b, Spitzer measured a day-side temperature of ~1200 K and night-side of ~970 K, with the hottest point shifted east of the substellar point by strong eastward equatorial winds.

The stellar initial mass function was first determined empirically for nearby stars in the solar neighbourhood by Edwin Salpeter in 1955, who found the number of stars N at a given mass M scales as dN/dM ∝ M^-2.35 for solar-mass and higher mass stars. The Salpeter slope means that for every 100 stars formed below 1 solar mass, only about one star with mass above 10 solar masses is produced.

The Sagittarius A* infrared flares observed by the GRAVITY instrument at the VLT have directly imaged, for the first time, hot blobs of gas (plasma 'hotspots') orbiting the black hole at about 30% of the speed of light at distances only 3–5 times the Schwarzschild radius. These observations directly probed the innermost stable circular orbit regime and provided new tests of Kerr black hole geometry.

The giant elliptical galaxy M87 — whose supermassive black hole (M87*) was imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope — also hosts one of the most powerful relativistic jets known, extending 5,000 light-years from the nucleus and visible from radio wavelengths to X-rays. The jet is powered by the spin of the black hole and the magnetic field in the accretion disc, thought to launch material via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism.

Vera Rubin and W. Kent Ford's 1980 paper presenting rotation curves of dozens of spiral galaxies — all showing the characteristic flat profiles inconsistent with the visible mass distribution — provided the definitive observational case that most of the mass in galaxies is dark. Rubin's meticulous observational work, though initially met with scepticism, ultimately transformed cosmology and earned her numerous honours before her death in 2016.

The future of the universe over vast timescales is determined by the properties of dark energy: if dark energy is a true cosmological constant, the universe will expand forever into an increasingly cold, dark, and lonely state — the 'heat death' or 'Big Freeze.' In about 100 trillion years all stars will have burned out; in 10^40 years all stellar remnants will have decayed; and in 10^67 years even stellar-mass black holes will have evaporated via Hawking radiation.
